teile.einleitung: Deep sleep is the most restful phase of sleep. During this time it is hardest to wake someone, and the body is completely relaxed. It is important for growth, recovery and learning.
wichtigste: Slow delta waves in the brain are typical of deep sleep.
Most deep sleep occurs in the first half of the night.
A lot of growth hormone is released in deep sleep.
Pulse, blood pressure and breathing become slower.
In deep sleep, factual knowledge is consolidated in the memory.
With increasing age the share of deep sleep decreases.

abschnitte.text: With an **EEG** you can measure the electrical activity of the brain. In deep sleep it shows large, slow **delta waves**. That is why deep sleep is also called “slow-wave sleep”. In the current classification of sleep stages, which has applied since 2007, it is called **stage N3**. Before that people spoke of stages 3 and 4.

A night is made up of several **sleep cycles** of about an hour and a half. Each cycle leads from light sleep into deep sleep and then into **REM sleep**, in which you dream a lot. The longest phases of deep sleep come in the **first half of the night**. Towards morning there is hardly any deep sleep, but more REM sleep.

In deep sleep the body is at its most relaxed. **Heartbeat**, **blood pressure** and **breathing** become slow and even. The pituitary gland releases especially much **growth hormone**. It is important for the growth of children and for the repair of tissue. That is why enough sleep is especially important for young people.

In deep sleep, things learned during the day, such as **vocabulary** and **facts**, are consolidated in the memory. So if you sleep well after studying, you can remember better. If you are woken from deep sleep, you are often **groggy and confused** and need a few minutes to become clear-headed. This state is called **sleep inertia**.

Children and teenagers have especially much deep sleep. With increasing age it **decreases**. In older people sleep becomes lighter and is interrupted more often. This is a normal part of getting older.

gewusst: Sleepwalking mostly comes out of deep sleep and not out of the dreaming phase.
After a sleepless night, the body makes up mainly the deep sleep the following night.

teile.einleitung: T helper cells are white blood cells that direct the immune system. They hardly kill any germs themselves, but they give other defence cells the signals they need. Without them, the defence collapses.
wichtigste: T helper cells carry the co-receptor CD4.
They recognise fragments of germs on MHC class II molecules.
Th1 cells activate scavenger cells, Th2 cells help against worms.
Follicular T helper cells support B cells in the lymph nodes.
Regulatory T cells dampen immune reactions.
HIV attacks T helper cells in particular.
Interleukin-2 is an important growth factor for T cells.

abschnitte.text: T helper cells are also called CD4-positive T cells, after their surface molecule **CD4**. Their **T cell receptor** recognises small pieces of protein that other cells display on **MHC class II molecules**. These molecules mainly carry fragments of proteins that have been taken in, for example from bacteria. The co-receptor CD4 stabilises the bond with this **antigen-presenting cell**.

Once activated, T helper cells release messenger substances, the **interleukins**. **Interleukin-2** is especially important, as it encourages T cells to multiply strongly. In this way a large number of suitable defence cells is created in a short time. The helper cells act like an operations control centre that decides which kind of defence is needed.

**Th1 cells** mainly activate scavenger cells, the **macrophages**. This helps to kill germs that live inside cells, such as tuberculosis bacteria. **Th2 cells** release interleukin-4, interleukin-5 and interleukin-13. They promote the production of IgE and the defence against worms, but are also involved in **allergies**. **Follicular T helper cells** travel to the lymph nodes and help the **B cells** there to make better antibodies.

**Regulatory T cells** have a special job: they **dampen** immune reactions. In this way they slow down defence responses that go too far. They help to prevent **autoimmune diseases**, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue.

The **HI virus** uses the CD4 molecule as a way in and gradually destroys the T helper cells. Healthy people have about 500 to 1,500 CD4 cells per microlitre of blood. If the count falls **below 200**, it is called **AIDS**. Then the risk of serious infections rises sharply. With today's medicines the virus can be kept well under control.

gewusst: Because HIV attacks the operations control centre of the immune system, otherwise harmless germs can become dangerous.
The abbreviation CD stands for “Cluster of Differentiation”, a numbering system for surface molecules.

teile.einleitung: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. It mostly affects the lungs. In the past it was very widespread in Europe, and today it can be treated with medicines.
wichtigste: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria.
Robert Koch discovered the germ in 1882.
The lungs are affected most often.
It is treated with several antibiotics over at least six months.
In the past the disease was called consumption.
Davos became famous through its sanatoriums for people with lung disease.

abschnitte.text: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria, above all by **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**. The bacteria are mostly passed on through fine droplets in the air when someone **coughs**. **Pulmonary tuberculosis** is the most common form. But the bacteria can also attack bones, lymph nodes or other organs. Worldwide, tuberculosis is still today among the infectious diseases with the most deaths.

The German doctor **Robert Koch** presented in Berlin on **24 March 1882** that bacteria cause tuberculosis. For his research he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 1905. In memory of his discovery, 24 March is today **World Tuberculosis Day**. In the past the disease was called **consumption**, because the sick people lost a great deal of weight and slowly “wasted away”.

In the 19th century people believed that fresh mountain air helps with tuberculosis. In **Davos** in the canton of the Grisons, many **sanatoriums**, that is health resorts for people with lung disease, were therefore built from about 1865. People from all over Europe travelled there to recover. In this way Davos became a famous health resort. Other mountain places such as Arosa or Leysin also became known through this.

Today tuberculosis is treated with **several antibiotics at the same time**, over at least **six months**. This prevents the bacteria from becoming resistant. It is important to take the medicines to the end. In **multidrug-resistant tuberculosis**, the most important standard medicines no longer work. Treatment is then much longer and more difficult.

With the **tuberculin test** you can check whether the body has had contact with the germ. In it, a protein of the bacteria is injected into the skin. If a hardening forms after a few days, the test is positive. The vaccination is called the **BCG vaccination**, named after the Frenchmen Calmette and Guérin. In Switzerland it is today recommended only in special cases.

gewusst: The famous novel “The Magic Mountain” by Thomas Mann is set in a sanatorium in Davos.
Tuberculosis is a very old disease: traces of it have been found even in mummies from ancient Egypt.

teile.einleitung: Translation is the step in which a protein is made from the building instructions of an mRNA. It takes place at the ribosomes. In it, amino acids are linked into a chain in the right order.
wichtigste: Translation takes place at the ribosomes.
Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, bacterial ones 70S.
The anticodon of the tRNA matches the codon of the mRNA.
The amino acids are linked by peptide bonds.
The ribosome has three tRNA binding sites: A, P and E.
At a stop codon, a release factor detaches the finished chain.

abschnitte.text: The **mRNA** contains the information in groups of three building blocks, the **codons**. Each codon stands for an **amino acid** or for a stop signal. The start codon is called AUG. The molecules that bring the amino acids are called **tRNA**. Each tRNA has an **anticodon** that matches the codon exactly. This makes sure that the right amino acid is built in.

**Ribosomes** are the protein factories of the cell. Their size is given as a sedimentation coefficient: ribosomes of eukaryotes are **80S**, those of bacteria **70S**. This difference is important for some **antibiotics**, which specifically inhibit bacterial ribosomes. A ribosome has three binding sites: at the **A site** the loaded tRNA arrives, at the **P site** the growing chain hangs, and through the **E site** the empty tRNA leaves the ribosome.

First, an enzyme, the **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase**, loads each tRNA with the matching amino acid. This needs energy from **ATP**, and each amino acid has its own synthetase. In the ribosome the carboxyl group of one amino acid is linked to the amino group of the next. This is the **peptide bond**, in which water is split off.

For **stop codons** there is no matching tRNA. Instead a **release factor** binds and detaches the finished chain. Often several ribosomes work one behind the other on the same mRNA. This is called a **polysome**. In this way many copies of a protein are made in a short time.

Proteins for membranes or for export carry a **signal peptide** at the start. It is recognised, and the ribosome docks at the **rough endoplasmic reticulum**. In **bacteria** a few things are different: they have no nucleus, so ribosomes can start on the mRNA while it is still being copied. Transcription and translation take place there **at the same time**.

gewusst: Of the 64 possible codons, three are stop codons, and all the others stand for amino acids.
The most important part of the ribosome, which forms the peptide bond, consists of RNA and not of protein.

teile.einleitung: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products. It checks whether medicines and medical devices are safe, effective and of good quality before they may be sold in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Swissmedic has existed since 2002.
Its predecessor was the Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines (IKS).
The basis is the Therapeutic Products Act (HMG).
Swissmedic monitors side effects even after approval.
The Federal Office of Public Health decides on the prices of medicines.
Medicines in category E can be sold freely.

abschnitte.text: Until 2001, medicines were checked by the **Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines** (IKS), a joint body of the cantons. In 2002 **Swissmedic** began its work together with the new **Therapeutic Products Act** (HMG). The law regulates the approval, manufacture, supply and monitoring of medicines and medical devices. Swissmedic is based in Bern.

Before a new medicine may be sold, Swissmedic checks its **safety**, **effectiveness** and **quality**. Even after approval, rare side effects can appear. Professionals and patients report suspected cases, and Swissmedic evaluates them. This task is called **pharmacovigilance**. The price of a medicine and whether health insurance pays for it are decided instead by the **Federal Office of Public Health**.

Medicines are sorted into **supply categories**. For some you need a doctor's prescription. Others are only available at a pharmacy or chemist's with expert advice. Medicines in **category E**, such as certain lozenges, may also be sold in shops without expert advice. This makes sure that strong medicines are used correctly.

Swissmedic regularly warns against ordering from unknown **online shops** abroad. Many medicines offered there are **fakes** with the wrong dose or dangerous ingredients. Customs often stops such parcels. It is safer to get medicines from a pharmacy or from a doctor.

gewusst: Swissmedic is also responsible for medical devices, for example plasters or blood sugar meters.
Fake medicines often look exactly the same as the real ones.

teile.einleitung: Everyone is sometimes sad, disappointed or has hurt themselves. Then comfort does you good. To comfort someone means to be there for them and to show them that they are not alone.
wichtigste: Comfort helps when someone is sad or in pain.
When comforting someone, listening well is especially important.
A hug can calm you down.
Small children find comfort in a cuddly toy.
You can also comfort yourself.
Therapy dogs visit people in care homes and hospitals.

abschnitte.text: Comfort is everything that helps a sad person to feel a little better again. It can be a kind word, a hug or simply that someone is there. Often you hand a crying person a **tissue**. That is a small, kind gesture. Comforting does not mean that the problem is gone at once, but you no longer carry it alone.

When comforting someone, **listening** is especially important. Someone who listens shows the other person that their worries are taken seriously. You do not always have to give advice straight away. Often it helps just to ask: “Do you want to tell me what happened?” It is also important not to play down feelings. It is allowed to be sad.

Small children often find comfort when going to sleep with a soft **cuddly toy**. It gives them a feeling of safety. If a child has hurt their knee, parents often **blow** on the spot. This distracts them and shows care. Someone who loses a game sometimes gets a **consolation prize**. That makes the disappointment a little smaller.

When you are hugged or cuddled, the body releases a messenger substance, **oxytocin**. It is often called the “cuddle hormone”. Oxytocin calms you and gives a feeling of closeness and trust. Animals can also comfort: specially trained **therapy dogs** visit people in care homes or hospitals. They let themselves be stroked, and that does many people good.

You can also **comfort yourself**. It helps to think of something nice, to listen to music, to draw or to move about. A conversation with a friend, your parents or a teacher can also help. Children and young people in Switzerland can also ring the number **147** of Pro Juventute free of charge at any time if they have worries.

gewusst: The German word “Trost” (comfort) is related to “treu” (loyal) and used to mean firmness and support as well.
Even stroking an animal can calm people and give them a good feeling.

teile.einleitung: Thalassaemia is an inherited disease of the blood. In it the body makes too little of the building blocks from which the red blood pigment haemoglobin is made. Depending on the form, you hardly notice it, or you need treatment for life.
wichtigste: In thalassaemia too few globin chains are made, but their shape is usually normal.
The name comes from the Greek word “thalassa” for sea, because the disease was first described in people from the Mediterranean region.
Small, pale red blood cells are typical.
The severe form of beta thalassaemia is also called Cooley's anaemia.
Many blood transfusions lead to iron overload in the body.
A normal ferritin level helps to tell mild thalassaemia from iron deficiency.

abschnitte.titel: What is missing in the blood
abschnitte.text: The **haemoglobin** in the red blood cells carries oxygen. It is made of protein chains, the **globin chains**, and of iron. In adults these are mainly two alpha chains and two beta chains. In thalassaemia, too little of one of these kinds of chain is made. If beta chains are missing, it is called **beta thalassaemia**, and if alpha chains are missing, **alpha thalassaemia**.

The building instructions for the chains are in the genes. A person normally has **four genes** for the alpha chain, two on each of the two chromosomes 16. The more of these that fail, the more severe the alpha thalassaemia. For the beta chain there are two genes. If only one is altered, the mild **thalassaemia minor** results, and if both are altered, the severe **thalassaemia major**.

In a blood count you see **small and pale** red blood cells, often also so-called target cells. This looks similar to iron deficiency. The difference shows in the **ferritin**, the stored iron: in thalassaemia it is normal or raised, in iron deficiency low. In beta thalassaemia minor the proportion of **HbA2** is also raised, usually above 3.5 per cent.

The mild form usually needs no treatment. The severe form, described in 1925 by the doctor Thomas Cooley, is therefore also called **Cooley's anaemia**. People with it often need regular **blood transfusions** even as children. With every transfusion, iron enters the body, and it is hardly excreted. Against this **iron overload** they take medicines called iron chelators. A stem cell transplant can cure the disease in some cases.

gewusst: Thalassaemia is especially common where malaria used to be widespread, because carriers are slightly better protected against malaria.
Many people with thalassaemia minor do not even know that they have this trait.

teile.einleitung: Drinking water is water that is so clean that you can drink it without worry. In Switzerland it comes out of the tap in top quality almost everywhere. Our body needs enough of it every day.
wichtigste: About four fifths of Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.
The rest comes mainly from lakes, and Zurich takes a lot of water from Lake Zurich.
The water supply, usually run by the municipality, brings the water to the houses.
Adults are advised to drink 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day.
Tap water is much cheaper than water in bottles.
You may drink from public fountains if there is no warning sign.

abschnitte.text: About **four fifths** of the drinking water in Switzerland comes from **springs** and **groundwater**. Rain and snow seep into the ground and are filtered naturally as they do so. The rest comes mainly from **lakes**. The city of Zurich, for example, takes most of its water from **Lake Zurich** and treats it in a waterworks.

abschnitte.titel: From the waterworks to the house
abschnitte.text: The **water supply** makes sure that water comes out of the tap. It usually belongs to the **municipality**. It collects the water, checks it regularly and sends it through pipes to the houses. In Switzerland drinking water counts as a **foodstuff** and has to meet strict rules. A litre of tap water costs only a fraction of a **centime**, while water in bottles is much more expensive.

**Thirst** is a signal from the body that it needs water. The **Swiss food pyramid** advises adults to drink **1 to 2 litres** of unsweetened drinks a day, ideally water. Children need a little less. When out and about, a **water bottle** that you fill at home with tap water helps. In the heat and when doing sport the body needs more.

In Swiss towns and cities there are many **public fountains**. Most of them have drinking water. Where the water is not drinkable, there is a sign saying **“Kein Trinkwasser”**, which means “not drinking water”. **Mineral water**, by contrast, is water from protected underground springs that contains minerals and is filled into bottles.

gewusst: The city of Zurich has over a thousand public fountains.
A large part of Swiss spring water is so clean that it hardly needs to be treated.

teile.einleitung: Tox Info Suisse is the national poisons information centre in Switzerland. Anyone who fears that someone has swallowed, breathed in or touched something poisonous can get advice there. The emergency number is 145.
wichtigste: Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich and advises the whole of Switzerland.
The emergency number 145 can be reached around the clock on every day.
Medicines are involved most often, followed by household products.
Among children, toddlers are affected most often.
With corrosive substances you should not make anyone vomit.
If someone is unconscious or has difficulty breathing, you dial 144 straight away.

abschnitte.text: Poisonings happen at any time of day. That is why the emergency number **145** of Tox Info Suisse can be reached **around the clock** and on every day. Experts answer the calls without a break. The centre is in **Zurich** and works closely with the **University of Zurich**. It advises not only private individuals but also doctors and hospitals.

Among children, **toddlers** are affected most often. They explore their surroundings with their mouths and easily swallow household products, parts of plants or tablets. **Medicines** are involved most often, because they are present in almost every household. They get mixed up, are given in too high a dose or are found by children. Next come **household products** such as cleaning agents.

When you phone, you keep the **packaging** of the product ready if possible. On it are the name and ingredients, so that the expert can assess the risk exactly. If a child has swallowed a **corrosive cleaning agent**, you should **not make them vomit**. Otherwise the liquid would damage the gullet a second time or get into the lungs.

**145** is for questions and advice about poisonings. But if the person is **unconscious** or is breathing badly, you dial **144** straight away, the ambulance service. The emergency call centre can, if needed, consult Tox Info Suisse itself. In hospital, **activated charcoal** is used for many poisonings, which binds poisonous substances in the gut. Whether this makes sense is decided by an expert.

gewusst: Activated charcoal has a huge inner surface to which many substances stick.
In many cases Tox Info Suisse can give the all-clear over the phone, so that no visit to the doctor is needed.

teile.einleitung: **Soap bubbles** are shimmering spheres made of a wafer-thin skin of soapy water. Inside is only air. With a little practice you can blow small and even huge bubbles.
wichtigste: A soap bubble is air in a thin skin of soapy water.
You mostly blow it through a small ring.
Slow, even blowing gives big bubbles.
In damp air, soap bubbles last longer.
Two bubbles that touch share a common wall.
Many tiny bubbles together are called foam.

abschnitte.text: If you dip a **small ring** into soapy water, a thin skin forms in it. If you blow through it, the skin bulges outwards. Finally it detaches and becomes a **sphere**. If you blow **slowly and evenly**, the skin can stretch calmly, and the bubble becomes big. Strong blowing, on the other hand, gives many small bubbles.

The soap skin contracts, like a stretched rubber band. In doing so it takes on the shape that needs the least skin for the same amount of air. This shape is the **sphere**. That is why free-floating soap bubbles are round. If two bubbles touch, they stick together and share a **common flat wall**. This is how a double bubble arises.

Soap bubbles shimmer in many **colours**. This comes from the light being reflected at the inside and the outside of the thin skin. The two parts of the light overlap and produce coloured patterns. The smooth surface also acts like a **small mirror ball**. In it you see the room or the sky small and curved.

Inside there is only air, but the skin of soapy water has a little **weight**. That is why a bubble slowly sinks to the ground after a while. Over time, water evaporates from the skin, it becomes thinner and bursts. In **damp air** it dries out less quickly and lasts longer. Dust or a dry hand also make it burst quickly.

Very many tiny soap bubbles that stick together form **foam**. You know it from the bath. When playing, no soapy water should get into the **eyes**. Soap irritates the sensitive eyes, and it stings. Then it is best to rinse them with clear water.

gewusst: The skin of a soap bubble is in places much thinner than a hair.
In great cold, soap bubbles can freeze and then form delicate ice patterns.

teile.einleitung: Triage means sorting injured or sick people by how urgently they need treatment. It is used when there are more patients than can be treated at once. This is meant to save as many people as possible.
wichtigste: The word “triage” comes from the French “trier”, meaning to sort.
The founder of modern triage is considered to be Napoleon's military surgeon Dominique-Jean Larrey.
Red means immediate treatment, yellow urgent, green lightly injured.
In the START scheme, anyone who can walk by themselves goes into the green category.
The Manchester Triage System sorts patients in the emergency department into 5 levels.
MANV stands for mass casualty incident.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the French verb **“trier”**, which means to sort or pick out. The founder of modern triage is considered to be **Dominique-Jean Larrey**, a military surgeon of Napoleon's. He had the wounded treated by the **severity of their injury** and not by their rank. He also introduced fast transport carriages for the wounded.

In a **mass casualty incident**, **MANV** for short in German, there are more injured people than rescue resources. Then triage becomes the most important task of the first emergency workers. The injured are given colours: **red** means immediate treatment is needed, **yellow** urgent and **green** lightly injured. **Blue** is a difficult category: it is used only if the resources are not enough for everyone and there is hardly any chance of survival. These people are cared for and assessed again as soon as more help arrives.

The **START scheme** helps to sort people quickly. Anyone who can **walk by themselves** goes into the **green** category and is sent to a collecting point. Then you check the breathing: more than **30 breaths per minute** means **red**. You also check the circulation. You press on a fingernail bed and measure how quickly it turns pink again. If this takes longer than **2 seconds**, it points to shock.

Triage is also carried out in hospital, so that the most urgent cases are seen first. A widespread method is the **Manchester Triage System**. It sorts patients into **5 levels**. Each level has a colour and a maximum waiting time until first contact with a doctor. Red means immediately, blue can wait the longest. That is why minor cases sometimes have to wait a long time in the emergency department.

gewusst: In major incidents the injured often get a coloured card or tag, so that all helpers can see the sorting at once.
Triage is repeated regularly, because a person's condition can change quickly.

teile.einleitung: The sense of touch is the sense with which we feel touch, pressure, warmth, cold and pain through the skin. It helps you, for example, to feel whether something is hot or cold. Its sense organ is the skin, our largest organ.
wichtigste: With the sense of touch we feel touch, pressure, vibration, warmth and cold through the skin.
It helps you to feel whether something is hot or cold.
In the skin lie different sensory cells, the receptors.
Fingertips, lips and tongue are especially sensitive.
The sense of touch is the first sense to develop in an unborn child.
Pain warns us of injuries.
Blind people read Braille with their sense of touch.

abschnitte.titel: What is the sense of touch?
abschnitte.text: The **sense of touch** is one of the five classic senses. Experts also speak of **haptic perception**. It tells us whether something is rough or smooth, soft or hard, wet or dry. Often the sensing of temperature and pain are counted as part of it too. Its sense organ is the skin, which in adults is about 1.5 to 2 square metres in size.

In the skin lie different **receptors**, each of which reacts to something particular. Some report light touch, others strong pressure or vibration. **Thermoreceptors** report warmth and cold, which is why you feel whether the soup is hot. Free nerve endings report pain. There are also nerves at the roots of the hairs, which is why you feel it when an insect crawls over your arm.

The touch receptors are not spread out evenly. There are especially many in the **fingertips**, the lips and the tongue. On the back they lie much further apart. You can test this: touch someone with two pencil points. On a finger you feel two points, on the back often only one. This test is called the **two-point test**.

The sense of touch is the first sense to develop, just a few weeks after conception in the womb. Newborns explore the world with their hands and mouth. Touches such as cuddling calm them and are very important for babies' development. In the process the body releases the hormone **oxytocin**. It strengthens the feeling of closeness and trust.

abschnitte.titel: The sense of touch in everyday life
abschnitte.text: With the sense of touch we button up shirts and find the light switch in the dark. **Pain** warns us so that we take our hand off the hot cooker ring in time. Blind people read **Braille**, made of raised dots and invented by the Frenchman Louis Braille. Smartphones also use the sense of touch when they vibrate. Many animals, such as cats with their whiskers, also feel very finely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensory cell that detects a particular stimulus.
A sensory cell in the skin that feels warmth or cold.
To do with touching and feeling.
A writing system of dots for blind people, which is read with the fingers.

gewusst: Louis Braille invented his dot writing system while still a teenager.
An adult's skin weighs several kilograms, which makes it the heaviest organ.
You can hardly tickle yourself, because the brain predicts your own movement.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Paraplegic Centre is a large specialist clinic for people with a spinal cord injury. It stands in Nottwil in the canton of Lucerne on Lake Sempach. There those affected are treated and prepared for an independent life.
wichtigste: The Swiss Paraplegic Centre stands in Nottwil in the canton of Lucerne.
It specialises in people with a spinal cord injury.
In a spinal cord injury, the spinal cord is damaged.
Those affected learn there to master everyday life anew, often in a wheelchair.
It is supported by the Swiss Paraplegic Foundation.

abschnitte.text: In the **spinal cord** run the nerve pathways between the brain and the body. If it is injured, for example in an accident, orders from the brain no longer arrive everywhere. Parts of the body can then no longer be moved and feel nothing. This is called **paralysis from a spinal cord injury**. If mainly the legs are affected, it is called **paraplegia**, which is where the centre’s name comes from.

The **Swiss Paraplegic Centre** lies in **Nottwil** in the canton of Lucerne. It opened in 1990 and is one of the large specialist clinics for spinal cord injury in Europe. There doctors, nursing staff, physiotherapists and occupational therapists work closely together. Besides treatment after the accident, it is about **rehabilitation**: those affected learn, for example, to move in a **wheelchair**, to dress themselves or to drive a car.

Behind the centre stands the **Swiss Paraplegic Foundation**, founded by the doctor Guido A. Zäch. A great many people in Switzerland support it as **donor members** with a yearly contribution. If they themselves have an accident and are paralysed afterwards, they receive financial support. In Nottwil, a lot of wheelchair sport is also done, including by top athletes.

gewusst: Nottwil lies directly on Lake Sempach.
Many Swiss wheelchair athletes who compete at the Paralympics train in Nottwil.

teile.einleitung: A university hospital is a hospital that works closely with a university. There, not only are sick people treated, but doctors are also trained and new treatments researched. In Switzerland there are five such hospitals.
wichtigste: University hospitals have three tasks: patient care, teaching and research.
Switzerland has five university hospitals.
They are in Zurich, Bern, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva.
The CHUV in Lausanne works together with the University of Lausanne.
The University Hospital Zurich belongs to the canton of Zurich.
Very complex procedures are shared out among a few centres.

abschnitte.text: A university hospital has three main tasks. First, **patient care**: it treats patients, often also with very serious or rare illnesses. Second, **teaching**: medical students learn here from experienced doctors. Third, **research**: experts look for new and better treatments.

In Switzerland there are five university hospitals. In **Zurich** stands the University Hospital Zurich, in **Bern** the Inselspital and in **Basel** the University Hospital Basel. In **Lausanne** lies the **CHUV**, the Centre hospitalier universitaire vaudois, the university hospital of the canton of Vaud. In **Geneva** there are the **HUG**, the Hôpitaux universitaires de Genève. They are among the largest hospital groups in Switzerland.

Health is in Switzerland mainly a matter for the **cantons**. The **University Hospital Zurich** is an independent public-law institution of the **canton of Zurich**. For teaching, it works together with the University of Zurich. The CHUV trains medical students together with the Faculty of Biology and Medicine of the **University of Lausanne**. Large hospitals such as the Cantonal Hospital of St Gallen also train people, but are not university hospitals.

Some procedures are very rare and difficult, for example **organ transplants**. Such treatments are called **highly specialised medicine**. The cantons coordinate them together and share them out among a few centres. The reason: someone who carries out a procedure often has more **experience** and routine, and this improves quality. Also, expensive equipment does not have to be built several times over in many hospitals.

gewusst: The Inselspital in Bern takes its name from a former monastery, the “Inselkloster” (island monastery), whose buildings it once took over.
At university hospitals often several thousand people work, many more than live in most Swiss villages.

teile.einleitung: An inactivated vaccine is a vaccine that contains no germs that can multiply. It trains the defence system without being able to cause the disease. Many important vaccinations in the Swiss vaccination schedule are inactivated vaccines.
wichtigste: Inactivated vaccines contain killed germs, parts of them or detoxified poisons.
They cannot multiply in the body and so cannot cause the disease.
A toxoid is a bacterial poison made harmless, for example for tetanus and diphtheria.
Usually several doses are needed, and boosters later.
The hepatitis B vaccine is made by genetic engineering in yeast cells.
The vaccination against TBE, which is passed on by ticks, is an inactivated vaccine.

abschnitte.text: A distinction is made between **live vaccines** and **inactivated vaccines**. Live vaccines contain weakened germs that can still multiply a little, for example against measles or chickenpox. **Inactivated vaccines**, by contrast, contain killed germs, only parts of them, or poisons that have been made harmless. They cannot multiply in the body and do not cause the disease.

With some diseases it is not the bacterium itself that makes you ill, but its **poison**. Then you vaccinate with a **toxoid**: the poison, for example the tetanus poison, is detoxified chemically but keeps its shape. In this way the body makes antibodies against it. Examples are the vaccinations against **tetanus** and **diphtheria**. **Subunit vaccines** contain only individual purified components, for example surface proteins. The **hepatitis B vaccine** contains a surface protein of the virus, which is made by genetic engineering, usually in **yeast cells**.

Because the components do not multiply, the stimulus for the immune system is **weaker** than with live vaccines. That is why the **primary immunisation** usually needs several doses. Later come **booster vaccinations**, for tetanus for example every few decades. Inactivated vaccines often also contain **adjuvants**, that is, helper substances that strengthen the immune response.

abschnitte.titel: Safe with a weak immune system
abschnitte.text: A big advantage: inactivated vaccines **cannot cause** the disease. That is why people with a weakened defence system may also be vaccinated with them. In them, however, the protection may be somewhat lower. Live vaccines, by contrast, are often not suitable for them.

In Switzerland **ticks** pass on **tick-borne encephalitis**, TBE for short. The TBE vaccination contains inactivated viruses and is an inactivated vaccine. According to the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH), in 2025 almost the whole of Switzerland except the canton of Ticino counts as a risk area. The vaccination is therefore recommended to many people who often spend time in the woods.

gewusst: The vaccination against polio that is used in Switzerland today is also an inactivated vaccine.
The diphtheria vaccination does not protect against the bacterium itself, but against its poison.

teile.einleitung: A tourniquet is a tying-off device for arms and legs. In first aid it is used only for life-threatening bleeding that cannot be stopped in any other way. Used correctly, it can save lives.
wichtigste: A tourniquet is meant for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg.
It is applied a few centimetres above the wound, not over a joint.
If the source of bleeding is unclear, the rule is “high and tight”.
The time of applying it must be noted.
It is tightened with a twisting rod, the windlass.
Only medical professionals may loosen a tourniquet again.

abschnitte.text: Most bleeding can be stopped with **pressure** on the wound or a **pressure bandage**. A **tourniquet** is meant for cases where this is not enough or there is no time for it, for example with very heavy bleeding after an accident. It cuts off the flow of blood into the whole limb. At the same time you alert the emergency services on **144**.

With a visible wound, the tourniquet goes **a few centimetres above** the wound, on the side nearer the body. Over a **joint** the vessel cannot be reliably pressed shut. If the exact source of bleeding cannot be seen, you apply it **as high up the limb** as possible. By the rule “high and tight”, all possible bleeding points below it are covered.

Modern tourniquets have a twisting rod, the **windlass**. By turning it, the wide band tightens so strongly that the **artery** is pressed shut. Then you secure the rod in a holder. It is tight enough when the **bleeding stops** and no pulse can be felt below it any more. A tourniquet that is too loose only dams the blood up in the veins and can even make the bleeding worse.

After applying it, you write down the **time**, often directly on the tourniquet. This information is important for treatment in hospital. A correctly applied tourniquet is considered acceptable for about **two hours**, after which the risk of muscle and nerve damage rises clearly. Only **professionals** may loosen it, because otherwise the bleeding can start again.

gewusst: A thin cord is unsuitable as a substitute: it cuts in and often still does not press the artery shut completely.
Tourniquets are now part of the equipment of many emergency services and are practised in first aid courses.

teile.einleitung: Sweet is one of the basic tastes that we detect with our tongue. Almost everyone likes sweet things from a very young age. The sweet taste tells the body that a food contains energy.
wichtigste: Sugar makes food sweet.
Sweet is one of the basic tastes.
Even babies like sweet things especially.
Sweet tells the body: there is energy in here.
Ripe fruits such as bananas taste especially sweet.
You should brush your teeth after eating sweet things.

abschnitte.text: With our tongue we taste **sweet**, **sour**, **salty**, **bitter** and **umami**, a savoury taste. For this there are many tiny **taste buds** on the tongue. **Sugar** is what tastes sweet above all. It is found in fruit, honey and sweets. Even babies like the sweet taste especially.

Sugar gives the body **energy**, for example for the muscles and the brain. The sweet taste is therefore a signal: there is energy in here. In the past this helped people to find nourishing fruit. Today sweet things are everywhere, so you should only eat them in moderation.

As a fruit **ripens**, it produces more sugar and its taste becomes sweeter. Unripe fruit often tastes sour or tart. Ripe **bananas** contain a lot of sugar and so taste especially sweet. Ripe strawberries, grapes or apples also taste sweeter than unripe ones.

In warm countries a lot of sugar is made from **sugar cane**. This is a tall grass with sweet juice. In Switzerland sugar is made from **sugar beet**. **Maple syrup** is made from the sap of the **sugar maple**. The sap is boiled for a long time until a sweet syrup is left. **Honey** is sweet too, and bees make it from flower nectar.

In the mouth live **bacteria** that turn sugar into acid. This acid can make holes in the teeth, which is called **tooth decay**. That is why you should **brush your teeth** after eating sweets. Drinking water also helps to wash away leftover sugar.

gewusst: To make one litre of maple syrup you need a great deal of tree sap, about 40 litres.
Cats cannot taste sweetness at all.

teile.einleitung: **Skipping** is a simple game and good training at the same time. You need only a rope and a little space. Legs, arms and heart all work.
wichtigste: In skipping, mainly the calf muscles work.
You land softly on the balls of your feet.
The heart beats faster when jumping.
You turn the rope mainly from the wrists.
The handles should reach about to the armpits.
Good trainers cushion the jumps.

abschnitte.text: In skipping, you hop again and again off your toes. This work is done mainly by the **calf muscles**. Thighs, abdomen and arms help too. The muscles need a lot of oxygen, so the **heart beats faster** and you breathe more deeply. Skipping is therefore good **endurance training**.

You jump only a little high and land softly on the **balls of your feet**. This way the legs cushion the jump well. The heels hardly touch the ground. **Good trainers** dampen the many small jumps and give support. A floor of wood or rubber is better than hard concrete.

The **elbows** stay close to the body. You turn the rope mainly with small movements from the **wrists**, not with the whole arms. The right length is important too. If you stand in the middle of the rope, the handles should reach about to the **armpits**. If the rope is too short or too long, you trip easily.

There are many different jumps. You can jump on one leg, alternately or with crossed arms. In the **double under**, the rope swings **twice** under the feet during one jump. For this you have to jump higher and turn fast. Anyone who practises a lot can learn whole sequences of tricks.

On the playground, people often play with a **long rope**. Usually **two children** hold the ends and swing. The others run in and jump in the middle. Sometimes verses are sung and the jumps counted. The game promotes skill, rhythm and togetherness.

gewusst: Many boxers train with a skipping rope to get fast feet.
Skipping is also done as a competitive sport, with speed events and freestyle routines.

teile.einleitung: Gymnastics is a sport with jumps, rolls and exercises on apparatus. It makes the body strong and flexible and trains balance. In Switzerland, gymnastics in clubs has a long tradition.
wichtigste: In gymnastics you practise on the floor and on apparatus.
Typical exercises are the forward roll, cartwheel, handstand and shoulder stand.
Apparatus include rings, balance beam, high bar and trampoline.
Soft mats protect you when landing.
The Federal Gymnastics Festival takes place about every six years.
In 2025 it took place in Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: Many gymnastics exercises are done on the **floor** on a mat. In the **forward roll** you curl up round like a ball and roll over your back. In the **cartwheel** you first put your hands down and then your feet and turn sideways. In the **handstand** you support yourself on your hands, with your legs pointing straight up. In the **shoulder stand** you lie on your back and stretch your legs straight up.

On the **rings**, which hang from ropes from the ceiling, you swing or hang. On the narrow **balance beam** you practise balance. On the **high bar** and the **parallel bars** you turn and support yourself. On the **trampoline** you jump high into the air on a stretched sheet that hangs from springs. In competition, men compete on six and women on four apparatus.

Under the apparatus you lay thick, soft **mats**. They protect you if you fall or land. For difficult exercises a teacher helps and gives a **spot**, that is, supports or secures you. Before gymnastics you warm up, so that muscles and joints are ready. You learn new exercises step by step.

In almost every Swiss municipality there is a **gymnastics club**. The largest association is the **Swiss Gymnastics Federation**. About every six years the **Federal Gymnastics Festival** takes place. There many thousands of gymnasts meet for competitions and displays. In 2025 it took place in **Lausanne**. Gymnastics is also part of lessons at school.

gewusst: The founder of club gymnastics is considered to be Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, who set up a gymnastics ground in Berlin at the start of the 19th century. He was called “Turnvater Jahn”, the father of gymnastics.
Trampolining has been an Olympic sport since 2000.

teile.einleitung: Transcription is the first step by which a cell uses the information of a gene. In it a section of DNA is copied into an RNA. This copy later serves as the building instructions for a protein.
wichtigste: In transcription, DNA is copied into RNA.
In cells with a nucleus it takes place in the nucleus.
RNA polymerase starts at the promoter, which often contains a TATA box.
The coding-template strand is read.
In splicing, the introns are removed and the exons are joined.
The mRNA gets a 5' cap and a poly-A tail.

abschnitte.titel: A copy instead of the original
abschnitte.text: **DNA** is like a big book with all the blueprints. In cells with a nucleus, the **eukaryotes**, it stays safely in the **nucleus**. For the work, only a copy is made, the **mRNA** (messenger RNA). This process is called **transcription**. The finished mRNA is then carried out of the nucleus into the **cytoplasm**, where the proteins are made.

The enzyme that builds the RNA is called **RNA polymerase**. It begins at a particular place in front of the gene, the **promoter**. There first **transcription factors** bind, and then the polymerase. Many promoters in eukaryotes contain the **TATA box**, a short sequence just before the start point. It serves as a binding site for the transcription factors.

DNA has two strands. What is read is the **template strand**, also called the antisense strand. The polymerase assembles matching RNA building blocks. The RNA that results therefore has the same sequence as the other strand, the **coding strand**, only made of RNA building blocks and with uracil instead of thymine.

In eukaryotes a **pre-mRNA** is made first. It contains **introns**, sections that do not code, and **exons**. In **splicing**, the introns are cut out and the exons are joined. At the 5' end the mRNA gets a **cap** of modified guanine, and at the 3' end a **poly-A tail** made of many adenine building blocks. Both protect it from being broken down.

In **alternative splicing**, different exons are joined together as needed. In this way different mature mRNAs arise from one gene. A single gene can therefore code for **several protein variants**. This explains why humans, with comparatively few genes, can make a great many different proteins.

gewusst: Bacteria have no nucleus, so transcription there takes place directly inside the cell.
Some genes consist for the most part of introns, which are later cut out again.

teile.einleitung: The thymus is a small organ in the chest, just behind the breastbone. It belongs to the body's defence system. In the thymus, certain defence cells learn to tell friend from foe.
wichtigste: The thymus is one of the lymphatic organs, that is, part of the defence system.
In the thymus the T lymphocytes mature, which are named after it.
The immature precursor cells come from the bone marrow.
In the thymus, T cells learn to tell what belongs to the body from what is foreign.
In children the thymus is large, in adults it becomes small and partly turns into fat.
The thymus consists of two lobes.

abschnitte.text: The thymus lies in the upper chest behind the **breastbone** and in front of the heart. It consists of a left and a right **lobe**, which are divided into many small lobules. It is one of the **lymphatic organs**, like the lymph nodes and the spleen. So it serves defence and not digestion.

abschnitte.titel: The school of the T cells
abschnitte.text: All blood cells are made in the **bone marrow**. Some of the precursors of lymphocytes travel through the blood to the thymus. There they mature into **T lymphocytes**, T cells for short. The T stands for thymus. T cells recognise germs and help to fight them.

In the thymus there is strict testing. T cells that would attack the **body itself** are sorted out. What is left are cells that only fight **foreign substances**. In this way the defence system learns to tell what belongs to the body from what is foreign. If a working thymus is missing from birth, no mature T cells are made, and a **severe weakness of the immune defences** results.

In children the thymus is **large and active**, because during this time the store of T cells is built up. Later it shrinks. In adults it is much smaller and largely replaced by **fatty tissue**. The T cells that have already been made, however, go on protecting the body.

gewusst: In cooking, the thymus of young calves is known as sweetbread, called “Kalbsmilken” in Swiss German and “Kalbsbries” in Germany.
In proportion to the body, the thymus is largest in small children.

teile.einleitung: A graze arises when you scrape across a rough surface, for example when falling onto asphalt. This scrapes off mainly the top layer of skin. Grazes often hurt but usually heal well.
wichtigste: Grazes often arise when falling onto asphalt.
Mainly the top layer of skin is injured.
Especially often affected are the knees and elbows.
A dirty graze is first rinsed with clean water.
On a small graze you stick a plaster.
During healing a scab forms, which you do not pick off.
Knee pads protect when inline skating.

abschnitte.text: A **graze** arises when the skin slides over a rough surface. This often happens when **falling onto asphalt**, gravel or a sports field. This rubs off mainly the **top layer of skin**, the **epidermis**. Beneath it lie many fine nerves, so a graze stings a lot. Children get grazes especially often on **knees and elbows**, because you catch yourself with them when you fall.

Because the wound was in contact with the ground, **dirt and germs** often sit in it. They can cause an **inflammation**. That is why you first **rinse** a dirty graze with **clean water**. Small stones can be removed carefully. Then you disinfect the wound and stick a **plaster** on it. Large or very dirty grazes should be looked at by a doctor.

After a short time a **scab** forms on the wound, a crust of dried blood. It **protects the healing wound** like a natural plaster. Underneath, new skin grows. You should **not pick** the crust, otherwise the wound opens again and heals more slowly. When the skin is finished, the scab falls off by itself.

Anyone who rides inline skates, a skateboard or a scooter protects themselves with **knee pads**, **elbow pads** and wrist guards. A **helmet** also protects the head. Long trousers and sleeves also prevent many grazes. On wet or gravelly ground you go more slowly, because you slip more easily there.

gewusst: Because only the top layer of skin is injured, a graze usually leaves no scar.
Grazes often sting more than small cuts, because a larger area with many nerve endings is exposed.

teile.einleitung: Tarmed was the tariff used in Switzerland to bill outpatient medical services. It set out how much a consultation or an examination costs. From 2026 it was replaced by TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.
wichtigste: Tarmed applied to outpatient medical services.
It was used across Switzerland from 2004.
Every service was rated in tariff points.
The value of a tariff point differed by canton and contract.
Tarmed was a fee-for-service tariff.
Its successors are TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.

abschnitte.titel: One tariff for the whole of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: **Tarmed** governed how doctors' practices and **hospital outpatient departments** billed their outpatient services. Outpatient means that you go home again after the treatment. In 2004 Tarmed replaced the previous **cantonal doctors' tariffs** with one tariff for the whole of Switzerland. Tarmed was a **fee-for-service tariff**. Each individual service, for example five minutes of consultation or an examination, was billed separately.

abschnitte.titel: Tariff points and tariff point value
abschnitte.text: Every service was rated in **tariff points**. To get the price, you multiply the tariff points by the **tariff point value** in francs. An example: 40 tariff points times 0.95 francs makes 38 francs. The number of tariff points was the same across Switzerland, but the tariff point value was agreed regionally. So the same service did not cost the same everywhere.

Doctors' tariffs are negotiated first of all by the **tariff partners**. These are associations of doctors and hospitals on one side and the **insurers** on the other. Only if they cannot agree can the **Federal Council** step in. A different system applies to stays in hospitals for acute somatic care: since 2012, billing has used **SwissDRG** and **case-based flat rates**, that is a fixed amount depending on the diagnosis.

Over time Tarmed came to be seen as **out of date**, because medicine had changed a great deal. After long negotiations the Federal Council approved **TARDOC** and **outpatient flat rates** as successors. They replaced Tarmed from 2026. With flat rates, each individual service is no longer billed. Instead there is a fixed amount for a whole treatment.

gewusst: Every year, many millions of outpatient treatments in Switzerland were billed with Tarmed.
On a doctor's bill under Tarmed you could look up every single service with its tariff number.

teile.einleitung: The dead space is the part of the airways in which no gas exchange takes place. The air in it does enter the body, but it does not reach the air sacs of the lungs. That is why it matters for breathing how deeply and how fast you take in air.
wichtigste: The anatomical dead space of an adult amounts to about 150 millilitres.
It includes the nose, throat, windpipe, bronchi and bronchioles.
Air sacs that are ventilated but not supplied with blood make up the alveolar dead space.
Anatomical and alveolar dead space together make up the physiological dead space.
Shallow, fast breathing is not very effective, because a lot of air stays in the dead space.
A very long snorkel increases the dead space.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen enters the blood only in the **alveoli**, the tiny air sacs of the lungs. The routes leading there, that is the **nose**, **throat**, **windpipe**, **bronchi** and **bronchioles**, only pass the air on. They make up the **anatomical dead space**. In an adult this is about **150 millilitres**. This air goes in and out again with every breath without reaching the alveoli.

Sometimes alveoli are ventilated but **not supplied with blood**. Then they too take no part in gas exchange and make up the **alveolar dead space**. This is typical in a **pulmonary embolism**: a clot blocks a pulmonary artery, and the alveoli behind it no longer receive blood. Together, anatomical and alveolar dead space make up the **physiological dead space**. In a healthy person it is almost the same size as the anatomical one.

With the **Bohr dead space equation** you can calculate the dead space. It compares the content of **carbon dioxide** in the exhaled air with that in the air of the alveoli. From this you find out what share of a breath did not take part in gas exchange. The equation goes back to the Danish physiologist Christian Bohr.

The dead space stays the same size with every breath. In a normal breath of about half a litre, most of it reaches the alveoli. With **shallow, fast breathing**, however, the dead space makes up a much larger share, and little fresh air is left for the alveoli. A **long snorkel** is also additional dead space: you breathe in your own CO2-rich air again. That is why snorkels are short.

gewusst: As a rough rule of thumb, the anatomical dead space is about 2 millilitres per kilogram of body weight.
Breathing tubes and masks in medicine also increase the dead space, which is why they are built as short as possible.

teile.einleitung: Tendons are the strong ropes that connect muscles to bones. Without them a muscle could not move a bone. You can even see some tendons under your skin.
wichtigste: A tendon connects a muscle to a bone.
Tendons consist of strong, tough fibres and are very resistant to tearing.
A tendon cannot contract by itself, only the muscle can.
Tendons look whitish and shiny, muscles are red.
On the back of the hand you see tendons when you spread your fingers.
Too much strain can inflame a tendon.

abschnitte.text: A **tendon** is like a strong rope between muscle and bone. It consists of many strong **fibres** that lie close together. That is why it is tough and hardly stretchable. Tendons look **whitish** and shiny, while muscles are red. They withstand very large pulling forces without tearing.

abschnitte.titel: The muscle pulls, the tendon transmits
abschnitte.text: When a muscle tenses, it becomes shorter and pulls on its tendon. The tendon passes this pull on to the bone, and the bone moves. The tendon itself, however, **cannot contract**. It does not work itself but only passes on the force of the muscle. Muscle, tendon and bone together form a team.

If you spread your fingers, you see tendons stand out under the skin on the **back of the hand**. They run from the muscles in the forearm to the fingers. Many tendons of the hand glide in **tendon sheaths**. These are coverings that lie like a tunnel around the tendon. In them the tendon can glide easily back and forth.

Below the **kneecap** lies a strong tendon. When the doctor taps on it with a small hammer, the muscle at the thigh is briefly stretched. In response it contracts in a flash, and the lower leg shoots forwards. This is called a **reflex**. This is how the doctor checks whether nerves and muscles work well together.

If a tendon is **strained too much** for a long time, it can become inflamed. This happens, for example, with movements that are always the same, such as a lot of typing or one-sided training. The spot then hurts and needs rest until it has recovered. Warming up before sport and breaks help to spare tendons. The largest tendon in the body is the **Achilles tendon** at the heel.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone and is the strongest tendon in humans.
Tendons have a poorer blood supply than muscles, which is why they heal more slowly.

teile.einleitung: The eye catches light, but we only see with the brain. The connection between them is the **optic nerve**. It carries the signals from the retina to the brain.
wichtigste: The optic nerve carries the signals from the eye to the brain.
It contains about a million nerve fibres.
The optic nerve is the second of the twelve cranial nerves.
In the optic chiasm, about half of the fibres change sides.
The exit point in the eye is called the optic disc.
Glaucoma can damage the optic nerve.

abschnitte.titel: From the eye to the brain
abschnitte.text: In the **retina**, sensory cells turn light into electrical signals. Nerve cells of the retina bundle these signals. Their long extensions together form the **optic nerve**. It contains about **a million nerve fibres**. It carries the signals from the eye backwards into the brain, as far as the visual cortex at the back of the head.

Humans have **twelve cranial nerves**, which emerge directly from the brain. They are numbered with Roman numerals. The olfactory nerve is cranial nerve I, the optic nerve **cranial nerve II**. Strictly speaking, the optic nerve is even an advanced part of the brain. That is why it is also wrapped by the meninges.

Behind the eyes, the two optic nerves meet in the **optic chiasm**, in Latin **chiasma opticum**. There about half of the fibres change to the other side. This way each half of the brain gets information from both eyes. This is important for spatial vision. After that the fibres run on as the optic tract to the brain.

abschnitte.titel: The optic disc and the blind spot
abschnitte.text: The place where the optic nerve leaves the eye is called the **optic disc**. It is round and bright. Eye doctors can see it well with the **ophthalmoscope**. At this place there are no sensory cells. That is why the **blind spot** arises there, which we do not notice in everyday life, though.

In **glaucoma**, also called **green star**, fibres of the optic nerve die off little by little. Often too high a pressure in the eye is the cause. Because you do not notice it for a long time, regular check-ups with the eye doctor are important. If the optic nerve of one eye is completely severed, that eye is **blind**. The signals from the retina then no longer reach the brain, and dead fibres do not grow back.

gewusst: The optic nerve is only about as thick as a pencil and yet carries about a million fibres.
Because the optic nerve belongs to the brain, doctors looking at the optic disc can sometimes even see signs of diseases in the head.

teile.einleitung: Grief is the feeling we have when we lose a loved person or animal. It is completely natural and shows how important someone was to us. Grief feels a little different for every person.
wichtigste: Grief is a natural reaction to a loss.
At a funeral you say goodbye to someone who has died.
In Switzerland many people wear black at a funeral.
The dead are buried in a cemetery.
Flowers and candles are signs of remembrance.
Talking together about the past can comfort you.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is grieving is sad and has **sorrow**, that is worries and a heavy heart. Grief takes a lot of strength. Many people then feel **tired and heavy**, some cannot sleep well or have no appetite. Besides sadness there is often anger, fear or even moments of joy. All these feelings are normal.

At a **funeral**, family and friends come together to say goodbye. In Switzerland the memorial service is also often called an **“Abdankung”**. Many people wear **black** clothes, because black is the colour of mourning with us. In other countries and cultures this can be different, where people wear white, for example.

The dead are buried in a **cemetery**. You can go there to think of them. Often you lay **flowers** on the grave. A burning **candle** is a sign of remembrance and of hope. After a great disaster, **flags are sometimes flown at half-mast**, that is raised only halfway, as a sign of mourning.

It helps children when they may ask questions and get honest answers. **Talking together about the past** keeps the person alive in the heart and comforts. Some people draw a picture, write a letter or look at photos. If you cannot talk to anyone, you can find help around the clock in Switzerland on the number **147** of Pro Juventute.

gewusst: Grief does not always follow the same course. After weeks or months it can suddenly become stronger again, for example on a birthday.
Many people also grieve deeply when they lose a pet.

teile.einleitung: Swimming is one of the most popular sports and an important skill. Anyone who can swim is safer in the water. In Switzerland, with its many lakes and rivers, this is especially important.
wichtigste: In backstroke you lie on your back.
The butterfly is named after an insect.
In Switzerland the SLRG publishes the well-known bathing rules.
You do not jump into cloudy, unknown water.
You do not run at the poolside, because it is slippery.
An Olympic swimming pool is 50 metres long.
The lifeguard looks after the bathers.

abschnitte.text: There are four well-known swimming strokes. In **breaststroke** you lie on your front and move arms and legs at the same time like a frog. In **front crawl** the arms pull alternately through the water, it is the fastest stroke. In **backstroke** you lie on your back. The **butterfly**, also called the **dolphin**, is named after an insect, because the arms swing forward like wings at the same time.

In Switzerland, the **SLRG**, the Swiss Life Saving Society, publishes the well-known **bathing rules**. One of them reads: **do not jump into cloudy, unknown water**, because there may be stones or shallow spots beneath. Further rules say that you should never swim long distances alone and should always supervise small children in the water within reach. You should also not go into the water on a full or completely empty stomach. The SLRG also trains lifeguards.

At the swimming pool, the **lifeguard** looks after the bathers. At the **poolside you do not run**, because the wet floor is **slippery**. Small children who cannot yet swim wear **armbands**. These never replace supervision by adults, though. Many children learn to swim in school swimming or in a swimming course.

**Swimming** has been Olympic since the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. An **Olympic swimming pool** is **50 metres** long. There are competitions in all swimming strokes and over different distances. Swimming trains almost all muscles and is easy on the joints, because the water carries the body. That is why it is a healthy sport for people of any age.

gewusst: An Olympic pool holds several million litres of water.
In many Swiss cities, hundreds of people swim in summer in rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare.

teile.einleitung: Many hormones cannot get into a cell. They deliver their message on the outside, and a second messenger substance inside the cell carries it on. This inner messenger is called a **second messenger**.
wichtigste: A second messenger carries a signal from the cell membrane into the cell interior.
The best-known second messenger is **cAMP** (cyclic adenosine monophosphate).
The enzyme adenylate cyclase makes cAMP from ATP.
A G protein links the hormone receptor with adenylate cyclase.
cAMP switches on protein kinase A.
Another second messenger is IP3, which releases calcium in the cell.
Signal cascades amplify a weak signal very strongly.

abschnitte.text: Peptide hormones such as **glucagon**, and adrenaline too, are water-soluble. The cell membrane, however, consists of a fat-like double layer through which such substances cannot pass. That is why the hormone binds on the outside to a **receptor**, a kind of receiving antenna. The receptor then passes the message on inwards. There a small molecule, the second messenger, takes over the distribution of the signal.

If a hormone binds to a **G protein-coupled receptor**, a G protein is activated inside the cell. It switches on the enzyme **adenylate cyclase**. Adenylate cyclase converts ATP, the cell’s energy carrier, into cAMP. cAMP binds to **protein kinase A** and releases its active parts. These attach phosphate groups to other proteins and so change their work.

Besides cAMP there are other second messengers. **IP3** (inositol trisphosphate) arises from a building block of the cell membrane. It travels to the **endoplasmic reticulum**, a store inside the cell. There it opens channels, and calcium streams into the cell plasma. The calcium then triggers various reactions, for example the contraction of muscle cells.

A single hormone molecule activates many enzyme molecules. Each of these enzymes in turn makes many cAMP molecules. In this way a **signal cascade** arises, which amplifies the signal step by step. From a tiny stimulus comes a large response of the cell. So that the signal also ends again, enzymes called **phosphodiesterases** break down cAMP.

The American **Earl W. Sutherland** found out that hormones such as adrenaline mediate their effect through cAMP. For this discovery he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1971. Later it turned out that caffeine too can inhibit the phosphodiesterases. Then cAMP lasts longer. At the amounts in coffee, though, caffeine acts mainly by blocking adenosine receptors.

gewusst: A single hormone molecule can trigger, through the cascade, the making of very many cAMP molecules.
The same cAMP can have quite different effects in different cells, depending on which proteins are present there.

teile.einleitung: The sympathetic nervous system is part of the autonomic nervous system. In times of stress and danger it prepares the body for action, without our controlling it consciously.
wichtigste: The sympathetic nervous system belongs to the autonomic nervous system.
It is especially active in times of stress and danger.
It speeds up the heartbeat and widens the pupils.
It widens the airways and slows down digestion.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline in the process.
The sympathetic trunk runs along both sides of the spine.

abschnitte.text: The **autonomic nervous system** controls the organs without our will, for example the heart, breathing and digestion. It consists of the **sympathetic nervous system**, the **parasympathetic nervous system** and the enteric nervous system of the gut. The sympathetic and parasympathetic systems mostly work as opposites. The sympathetic system is the accelerator, the parasympathetic system the brake for rest and recovery.

In times of stress and danger, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for **fight or flight**. It raises the **heart rate** and **blood pressure** so that the muscles get more blood. It widens the **airways** so that more air flows into the lungs. The **pupils** become wider so that more light enters the eye.

In a dangerous situation, digesting is not important. So the sympathetic nervous system **slows down** the activity of the stomach and gut. The flow of saliva also decreases, which is why your mouth goes dry when you are excited. The energy goes instead to the muscles, heart and brain.

On both sides of the spine runs a chain of nerve knots, the **sympathetic trunk**. There many sympathetic nerve fibres are switched over before they travel on to the organs. At the nerve endings the messenger substance **noradrenaline** is at work. In addition, the **adrenal medulla** releases **adrenaline** into the blood. It strengthens the effects of the sympathetic nervous system throughout the body.

gewusst: The sweat glands are also controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, which is why you sweat when you are excited.
The name comes from Greek and means roughly “feeling with”.

teile.einleitung: Sebaceous glands are small glands in the skin. They make sebum, a mixture of fats that keeps skin and hair supple and protects the skin.
wichtigste: Sebaceous glands make skin oil, called sebum.
Most of them open into the hair follicle.
There are no sebaceous glands on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet.
There are especially many on the face, chest and back.
Sebaceous glands work holocrine: whole cells break down into sebum.
The Meibomian glands on the edge of the eyelid are special sebaceous glands.

abschnitte.text: **Sebum** is a mixture of different fats. Together with sweat it forms a thin **protective film** on the skin. This film keeps the skin supple, protects it from **drying out** and holds back many germs. Sebum also makes the hair soft and shiny.

Most sebaceous glands open into the **hair follicle**, the sheath around the hair. From there the sebum reaches the surface of the skin. The sebaceous glands of the scalp give off sebum constantly. It spreads along the hairs. That is why hair gets **greasy** if you do not wash it for a long time.

Especially many sebaceous glands sit on the **face**, above all in the so-called **T-zone** of forehead, nose and chin, and on the **chest**, the **back** and the scalp. There the skin gets shiny more quickly. On the **palms of the hands** and **soles of the feet**, by contrast, there are no hairs and no sebaceous glands either. In teenagers the glands often produce a lot of sebum, which can lead to spots.

Sebaceous glands work **holocrine**. This means that the gland cells fill up with fat, die and break down. Their whole contents become sebum. New cells grow back all the time. A special form is the **Meibomian glands** on the edge of the eyelids. They release fat into the tear film so that the tear fluid on the eye does not evaporate too quickly.

gewusst: On each eyelid, several dozen Meibomian glands sit side by side.
The word holocrine comes from Greek and means roughly “secreting entirely”.

teile.einleitung: Thermogenesis means heat production. Our body constantly produces heat so that it can keep a temperature of about 37 degrees. This heat arises when we digest food, when we move and, in the cold, also in special ways.
wichtigste: Processing food costs about 10 per cent of the daily energy turnover on a mixed diet.
Protein needs the most energy to be processed, fat the least.
In the cold, muscle shivering quickly produces extra heat.
Non-shivering thermogenesis is especially important in newborns.
Thyroid hormones raise the basal metabolic rate and heat production.
The hypothalamus in the brain controls body temperature.

abschnitte.text: When you eat, you use energy for the digestion, absorption and processing of nutrients. This is called **diet-induced thermogenesis**. On a mixed diet it is about **10 per cent** of total turnover. With **protein**, around 20 to 30 per cent of the energy taken in is needed for processing, and with fat the share is smallest. That is why you sometimes feel warm after a big meal.

When we are cold, we start to shiver. In **cold shivering** the muscles contract quickly and in a disorderly way. They do no work in the process, and the energy becomes almost entirely **heat**. There is also **non-shivering thermogenesis**. Here energy in the metabolism is released directly as heat, mainly in **brown fat tissue**. Babies have especially much of it.

Every movement produces heat, because muscles convert only part of the energy into force. That is why we get hot when we do sport. Movement in everyday life counts too: walking, standing, climbing stairs or fidgeting. Experts call this **NEAT**, short for “Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis”. This share differs very much from person to person.

The temperature centre lies in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the brain. It compares the measured temperature with the set value and, when needed, starts heat production or cooling by sweating. The **thyroid hormones** thyroxine and triiodothyronine raise the activity of many cells. In an overactive thyroid, people often sweat and hardly ever feel cold.

gewusst: The substance 2,4-dinitrophenol used to be sold as a slimming aid. It is life-threatening, because the energy is released as heat instead of as ATP and the body can overheat.
Even in shivering, so much heat is released that the body's energy use rises clearly.

teile.einleitung: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear that has no outside source of sound. People with it hear, for example, a whistling, rushing or humming. For some it is there only briefly, while for others it stays with them for a long time.
wichtigste: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear without a sound source outside.
The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, meaning to ring.
Tinnitus is a symptom with various causes, not an illness of its own.
In teenagers, music that is too loud is a common cause.
From about three months' duration it is called chronic tinnitus.
Ear protection and distance from the speakers protect you at concerts.

abschnitte.text: With **tinnitus** you hear a whistling, rushing, droning or humming, although no matching sound comes from outside. The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, which means **to ring**. Almost all ear noises are **subjective**: only the person affected hears them, and they arise in the hearing pathway. Rarely there is an **objective tinnitus**, which others can also measure, for example an audible rushing of blood.

Tinnitus is a **symptom**, that is, a sign of illness. It can appear after loud **noise**, in **sudden hearing loss** or with **stress**. In teenagers, **music that is too loud** is a common cause, for example in headphones or at concerts. Noise can damage the fine **hair cells** in the inner ear. A whistling after a concert is a warning sign.

At a loud concert it is best to protect yourself with **ear protection** and **distance from the speakers**. Ear protection lowers the sound level in the ear, and with every metre of distance it becomes quieter. With headphones it helps to keep the volume low and to take breaks. In Switzerland there are legal rules on volume for events.

A tinnitus that lasts longer than about **three months** counts as **chronic**, and before that it is called acute tinnitus. Many people with it notice it especially strongly in **quiet surroundings**, for example when falling asleep, because other noises then do not cover it. In **cognitive behavioural therapy** you learn to pay less attention to the noise. In this way the brain often gets used to it.

gewusst: Many people hear a faint ear noise after a while in a completely quiet room.
A quiet background noise, such as a fan, can help you notice the tinnitus less when falling asleep.

teile.einleitung: Surprise is a feeling that arises when something unexpected happens. It comes suddenly and usually lasts only a short time. Afterwards another feeling often follows, for example joy or fear.
wichtigste: A surprise arises when something unexpected happens.
It usually lasts only a short time.
In a surprise the mouth often opens.
A typical exclamation is “Oh!”.
A sudden, unpleasant surprise is called a fright.

abschnitte.text: You can often recognise surprise by the face. The **eyebrows** go up, and the eyes become wide. The lower jaw drops slightly, and the **mouth opens** into an “oh”. Many people then also call out “Oh!” or “Wow!”. That is why people say “my **jaw dropped**” when they are very surprised.

A surprise is over quickly, often after a few seconds. Afterwards you realise what has actually happened. Then usually another feeling follows. A nice surprise makes you **happy**. A spooky surprise makes you **afraid**. A sudden, unpleasant surprise, such as a loud bang behind your back, is called a **fright**.

Many people like to surprise others. At a **surprise party**, everyone secretly prepares a celebration, and the person being celebrated knows nothing about it beforehand. An unexpected present or a letter from a friend can also be a nice surprise. Someone who is very amazed at something new is **astonished**. Astonishment helps us to discover and learn new things.

gewusst: Researchers often count surprise among the basic feelings that people all over the world show in a similar way.
The face shows surprise so quickly that you can hardly prevent it.

teile.einleitung: The subcutaneous tissue is the lowest layer of the skin. It consists mainly of fatty tissue and loose connective tissue. It warms, cushions and stores energy for the body.
wichtigste: The subcutaneous tissue is the lowest layer of the skin.
It consists mainly of fatty tissue.
