The fat protects against cold and stores energy.
Fat cells are called adipocytes in technical language.
At the heel the fat pad acts like a shock absorber.
Pacinian corpuscles in the subcutaneous tissue feel vibrations.

abschnitte.text: The skin consists of three layers. At the very top lies the **epidermis**, below it the **dermis** and at the bottom the **subcutaneous tissue**, called the **subcutis** in technical language. The subcutaneous tissue lies between the dermis and the muscle sheaths below. It connects the skin with the muscles and the bone membrane. Because it is loosely built, the skin can be moved about in many places.

The subcutaneous tissue consists mainly of **fatty tissue**. The fat cells are called **adipocytes**. They lie together in small lobules and store fat in large droplets. The **subcutaneous fat** acts like an insulating layer against cold. It is also an **energy store**: if the body needs more energy than it gets from food, it can draw on this reserve.

In some places the subcutaneous tissue is an important **cushion**. At the **heel** the fat pad is especially thick. It acts like a **shock absorber** with every step. Deep in the subcutaneous tissue also lie the **Pacinian corpuscles**. These sensory corpuscles react especially to **vibrations**, for example when the phone buzzes in your trouser pocket.

Some medicines are injected into the subcutaneous tissue. This is called a **subcutaneous injection**, from “sub” for under and “cutis” for skin. The medicine reaches the fatty tissue and from there is slowly taken up into the blood. This is how many people with **diabetes**, for example, inject their **insulin**. Some vaccinations are also given this way.

Many animals in cold regions have an especially thick subcutaneous layer. **Whales** and **seals** have a thick layer of blubber. This layer keeps them warm in the ice-cold sea water. It also serves as a reserve when the animals eat little for a long time. Polar bears and penguins also protect themselves with fat under the skin.

gewusst: In large whales the layer of blubber can be several dozen centimetres thick.
The subcutaneous tissue is not equally thick everywhere: on the eyelids the fat pad is almost entirely missing.

teile.einleitung: The University Children's Hospital Zurich is one of the largest children's hospitals in Switzerland. Many people simply call it the “Kispi”. There, children and teenagers are treated for minor and for very serious illnesses.
wichtigste: The Children's Hospital Zurich is called the “Kispi” for short.
It is one of the largest children's hospitals in Switzerland.
It treats children and teenagers.
As a university hospital it works together with the University of Zurich.
It is run by a private foundation.

abschnitte.text: At the **Kispi** work doctors, nurses and many other professionals who know especially much about **children and teenagers**. Children are not small adults: their bodies are still growing, and many illnesses take a different course. That is why children's hospitals of their own are needed. At the Kispi, children are treated for emergencies, for rare illnesses and also after serious accidents.

The children's hospital is a **university hospital**. It works closely with the **University of Zurich**. Young doctors learn there how to treat children. A great deal of **research** is also done, so that children's illnesses can be better understood and cured. The Kispi is run by a private foundation, the **Eleonorenstiftung**.

The Children's Hospital Zurich has existed since the 19th century. For a long time it stood in the Hottingen district. At the end of **2024** it moved into a large **new building** in Zurich-Lengg. The new building was designed by the Basel architects **Herzog & de Meuron**. It has a lot of wood and light and is meant to feel friendly for children and their families.

gewusst: Children in hospital often get visits from hospital clowns, who make them laugh and distract them.

teile.einleitung: Thermoregulation means that the body controls its own temperature and keeps it at about 37 degrees Celsius. Whether you are playing in the snow or running in the summer heat, your body makes sure that it does not get too cold or too warm inside. A red face when running or goosebumps in winter are visible signs of this.
wichtigste: The human body keeps its core temperature at about 37 degrees Celsius.
The temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus in the brain.
When you run you go red, because more blood flows to the skin to give off heat.
Sweating cools the body through evaporation.
In the cold we shiver to produce heat.
Humans, mammals and birds are warm-blooded.
A fever is a deliberate rise in body temperature.

abschnitte.text: **Thermoregulation** means regulating heat. The body constantly measures its temperature and balances out deviations. The temperature inside the body, the **core temperature**, is about 37 degrees Celsius in humans. The skin, hands and feet, by contrast, may be clearly cooler. Even a few degrees of deviation inside the body can become dangerous.

The control centre lies in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. It receives reports from temperature sensors in the skin and in the blood. Like the thermostat of a heating system, it compares the values with the set value. If it is too warm, it switches on cooling. If it is too cold, it makes sure there is more warmth.

When you run, your muscles produce a lot of heat. The blood vessels in the skin **widen**, and more blood flows to the skin to give off heat, which is why your face goes red. At the same time the sweat glands produce **sweat**. When it evaporates on the skin, it draws heat out of the body. That is why it is important to drink a lot in the heat.

In the cold the blood vessels of the skin **narrow** so that less heat is lost, and the skin turns pale. The muscles start to tremble, and this **cold shivering** produces heat. Goosebumps are also a reaction to cold, which in animals with thick fur makes the fur stand up. We also look for warm places and put on warm clothes. Babies additionally have brown fat tissue, which produces heat directly.

Humans, mammals and birds are **warm-blooded**, and they keep their temperature almost always constant. Lizards, snakes, fish and insects, by contrast, are **cold-blooded**. Their temperature depends on their surroundings, which is why lizards bask on warm stones in the morning. Marmots in the Alps greatly lower their body temperature during hibernation. This saves energy over many months.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature inside the body, about 37 degrees in humans.
The part of the brain that, among other things, controls body temperature.
Living things that keep their body temperature constant by themselves.
Animals whose temperature adapts to their surroundings.

gewusst: Dogs can hardly sweat and cool down mainly by panting.
Elephants use their big ears like radiators, through which a lot of blood flows.
Body temperature varies slightly over the day and is lowest in the early morning.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss vaccination schedule says which vaccinations are recommended at which age. It is published by the Federal Office of Public Health together with an expert commission and revised regularly. In Switzerland, vaccinations are in principle voluntary.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there is no general compulsory vaccination, vaccinations are in principle voluntary.
Basic vaccinations are recommended for everyone to protect personal and public health.
Supplementary vaccinations offer individual protection but do not count as basic for everyone.
Infants get the six-in-one vaccination at 2, 4 and 12 months.
The two MMR vaccinations are recommended at 9 and 12 months.
If the hepatitis B vaccination is missing, it is caught up between 11 and 15 years.
From 65 years, the yearly flu vaccination is recommended for everyone.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss vaccination schedule** is a list of recommendations. It is drawn up by the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** together with the **Federal Commission for Vaccination**. It says which diseases you should be vaccinated against and at what age. Doctors follow it. Because research goes on, the schedule is adjusted regularly.

The schedule distinguishes several groups. **Basic vaccinations** are recommended for everyone, because they protect one’s own health and that of the whole population. **Supplementary vaccinations** offer individual protection but do not count as basic for everyone. In addition there are vaccinations for **risk groups**, that is, for people who are especially at risk. One example: from **65 years**, the yearly **flu vaccination** is recommended for everyone.

Even infants are vaccinated against several diseases at the same time. The **six-in-one vaccination** protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, **polio**, **Haemophilus influenzae type b** and **hepatitis B**. It is given at **2, 4 and 12 months**. Against measles, mumps and rubella there is the **MMR vaccination**, recommended at **9 and 12 months**. Several doses are needed so that the protection lasts a long time.

If a vaccination was missed, you can usually **catch it up**. The vaccination against **hepatitis B**, for example, is recommended **between 11 and 15 years** if it was not given in infancy. In adolescence and adulthood too, some **booster vaccinations** are needed, for example against tetanus. In the **vaccination record**, every vaccination is entered, so you can see at any time what is still missing.

In Switzerland there is **no general compulsory vaccination**. Vaccinations are in principle **voluntary**, and each person, or for children the parents, decides for themselves. The experts recommend the basic vaccinations because they protect against severe diseases. When many people are vaccinated, some diseases can hardly spread any more. This also benefits people who cannot be vaccinated themselves.

gewusst: Thanks to vaccinations, polio has been regarded as eradicated in Europe since 2002.
The vaccination record also exists in electronic form.

teile.einleitung: An **eye test** measures how sharply someone sees. This is how you notice whether glasses are needed. There are eye tests for children, adults and, for example, before driving.
wichtigste: An eye test checks how well you see.
How sharply someone sees is called visual acuity.
On the eye chart, the characters get smaller and smaller.
Each eye is checked separately.
With Landolt rings you say where the ring is open.
In Switzerland you need an eye test for the learner driver’s permit.

abschnitte.text: In many eye tests you read characters on an **eye chart** on the wall. The characters get **smaller and smaller** from line to line. The smaller the characters someone can still make out, the better they see. In this way **visual acuity** is measured. It says how finely someone can tell things apart from a certain distance.

In the eye test you usually cover one eye. This way you can test **each eye separately**. Often one eye sees better than the other. You hardly notice this in everyday life, because the better eye makes up for a lot. Only in the test does the difference show.

Instead of letters, **Landolt rings** are often used. Each ring has a small gap. You say whether it is at the top, bottom, left or right. Small children who cannot read yet name **pictures** or show with their hand the direction of characters. This way their eyes too can already be tested well.

abschnitte.titel: Eye test for the driving licence
abschnitte.text: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive a car must first take an **eye test**. Only then do you get the **learner driver’s permit**. In road traffic, good sight is especially important. You have to recognise signs, traffic lights and other road users in time. Anyone who needs glasses must wear them when driving.

A simple eye test is done by **opticians**, for example in a glasses shop. For exact examinations and in diseases you go to the **eye doctor**. At school or at the paediatrician, sight is also sometimes checked. Children often do not notice themselves that they see poorly. That is why such tests are especially important.

gewusst: The Landolt rings are named after the Swiss eye doctor Edmund Landolt.
An eye test does not measure only sharpness: there are also tests for colour vision and spatial vision.

teile.einleitung: Trypsin is an enzyme that breaks down proteins from food in the small intestine. It is made in the pancreas, but first in a harmless precursor form. Only in the gut is it switched on.
wichtigste: Trypsin is a digestive enzyme for proteins.
The pancreas makes it as the precursor trypsinogen.
In the duodenum, enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen.
Trypsin cuts protein chains after lysine and arginine.
It belongs to the serine proteases.
It works best at about pH 8.

abschnitte.text: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical processes in the body. Trypsin is a **protease**, that is an enzyme that cuts other proteins into smaller pieces. Proteins consist of long chains of **amino acids**. Trypsin prefers to cut these chains after the amino acids **lysine** and **arginine**. Because it cuts so precisely, it is also happily used in the laboratory.

The **pancreas** does not make trypsin in finished form, but as an inactive precursor, **trypsinogen**. Active trypsin would otherwise attack the tissue of the pancreas itself. For safety there is also an inhibitor there, the **pancreatic trypsin inhibitor SPINK1**. It binds small amounts of trypsin that become active too early. Changes in its gene raise the risk of chronic inflammation of the pancreas.

In the **duodenum**, the enzyme **enteropeptidase**, also called enterokinase, sits in the lining. It cuts a short piece off trypsinogen, and active trypsin is formed. This then activates further precursors, for example **chymotrypsinogen** and procarboxypeptidases. This makes an **activation cascade**: one enzyme switches on many others.

Trypsin belongs to the **serine proteases**. In the active centre, that is the place where it works, sit three amino acids: **serine, histidine and aspartate**. They are called the **catalytic triad**. Aspartate aligns the histidine, the histidine activates the serine, and the serine attacks the bond between two amino acids. Trypsin works best in the slightly basic environment of the small intestine at about **pH 8**.

gewusst: The name trypsin goes back to the German researcher Wilhelm Kühne, who in the 19th century also coined the word “enzyme”.
In laboratories, trypsin is used to detach cells from the bottom of culture dishes so that they can be grown on.

teile.einleitung: Sugary drinks are drinks with a lot of added sugar, for example cola, lemonade or iced tea. They taste good, but often contain more sugar than you might think.
wichtigste: Half a litre of cola contains more than 10 sugar cubes.
Lemonade, cola and iced tea are sugary drinks.
Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.
Water and unsweetened tea are good ways to quench your thirst.
Squash should be diluted strongly with water.
Energy drinks are not suitable for children.

abschnitte.text: Half a litre of ordinary **cola** contains over 50 grams of sugar. That is more than **10 sugar cubes**. **Lemonade** and **iced tea** also contain a lot of added sugar. Because you cannot see the sugar in a drink, it is easy to drink a great deal of it. The fizzy bubbles in many sugary drinks come from **carbon dioxide**.

Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. This acid attacks the teeth and can make holes, which is called **tooth decay**. People who often drink sugary drinks, especially in small sips throughout the day, are more likely to get tooth decay. Too much sugar can also contribute to being overweight.

The best thirst quencher is **water**. In Switzerland you can safely drink tap water. A slice of **lemon** or a few mint leaves give water flavour without much sugar. **Unsweetened herbal tea** contains no sugar either. **Squash** is very sweet, so you dilute it strongly with water.

**Energy drinks** contain a lot of **caffeine** and sugar. For children this is not healthy. It can cause, for example, a racing heart, restlessness and sleep problems. That is why energy drinks are not suitable for children. They are also not a sports drink and do not quench thirst well.

gewusst: Even fruit juices without added sugar contain a lot of natural fruit sugar.
Swiss tap water is one of the most closely monitored foods.

teile.einleitung: A universal donor is a person whose blood can be given to almost everyone else. For red blood cells this is blood group O negative. Whether blood matches depends on features on the blood cells and on antibodies in the plasma.
wichtigste: For red blood cells, O negative is the universal donor.
AB positive is regarded as the universal recipient.
Plasma of group AB suits all recipients.
Anyone with blood group O has anti-A and anti-B in the plasma.
In an emergency, injured people get blood of group O negative first.
AB negative is the rarest blood group in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: On the **red blood cells** there can be features called **A** and **B**. Someone who has only A has blood group A, someone who has both has AB, and someone who has neither has group **O**. In the **plasma**, the liquid part of the blood, there are **antibodies** against the foreign features. A person with group A has anti-B, one with group O has anti-A and anti-B. When antibodies meet matching features, the blood **clumps together**.

abschnitte.titel: Why O negative is so in demand
abschnitte.text: Red blood cells of group O carry no A and B features. The recipient's antibodies therefore find nothing to direct themselves against. If the blood is also **Rhesus negative**, the feature **D** is missing too. That is why **O negative** counts as the **universal donor**. In serious accidents there is often no time to determine the blood group. Then injured people get blood of group O negative first.

People with **AB positive** have no antibodies against A, B or D. They therefore tolerate red blood cells of all groups and count as **universal recipients**. In reverse, people with O negative may receive only red blood cells from **O negative**. A person with group B has anti-A and tolerates only cells from **B and O**. With **plasma** it is the other way round: plasma of group **AB** contains neither anti-A nor anti-B and suits everyone.

In Switzerland **A positive** and **O positive** are the most common blood groups. The rarest is **AB negative**, which only about one per cent of the population has. Blood donation here is organised mainly by **Blood Donation SRK Switzerland** (Swiss Red Cross). Healthy adults may donate. Because blood keeps only for a limited time, new donors are needed again and again.

gewusst: The blood groups A, B and O were discovered by the Austrian doctor Karl Landsteiner in 1901. He later received the Nobel Prize for it.
Animals such as dogs and cats also have blood groups, only different ones from humans.

teile.einleitung: Tetanus, also known as lockjaw, is a dangerous disease caused by bacteria from the soil. They get into the body through wounds. A vaccination protects reliably.
wichtigste: Tetanus is also called lockjaw.
The bacteria live in the soil and in street dust.
A poison made by the bacteria causes severe muscle spasms.
Spasms of the jaw muscles are typical.
Tetanus does not pass from person to person.
Only your own vaccination protects you, even after you have had the illness.
Adults get a booster at the ages of 25, 45 and 65.

abschnitte.text: Tetanus is caused by the bacterium **Clostridium tetani**. It lives in the soil, in dust and in the gut of animals, and is present practically everywhere. The bacteria form very tough **spores** that can survive heat and dryness for years. If they get into the body through a dirty **wound**, they germinate. Even a small scratch while gardening can be enough.

The bacteria make a very powerful nerve poison, **tetanospasmin**. It disturbs the control of the muscles, which then cramp continuously. Tetanus often begins with **lockjaw**, so that you can hardly open your mouth. Later more muscles all over the body cramp. The illness has to be treated in hospital.

Tetanus is **not passed from person to person**. You only catch it through dirty wounds. That is why only your **own vaccination** protects you. Even someone who has survived tetanus is not immune afterwards. A tiny amount of poison is enough to cause the illness, but too little to build up protection. So you need a vaccination even after you have had the illness.

Children are vaccinated against tetanus as part of the **Swiss vaccination schedule**. For adults the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** recommends boosters at the ages of **25, 45 and 65**, that is every 20 years, and after that every 10 years. The tetanus vaccination is usually given as a **combined vaccine** with **diphtheria**, often also with whooping cough. After an injury, the doctor checks whether the vaccine protection is still enough.

gewusst: Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburo developed an antiserum against tetanus around 1890.
Tetanus spores can survive in the soil for many years.

teile.einleitung: Thrombocytes is the technical word for platelets. They are the smallest particles in the blood and have an important job: when you hurt yourself, they help the bleeding to stop.
wichtigste: Thrombocytes are called platelets in everyday language.
They are the smallest blood cells and have no cell nucleus.
They are made in the bone marrow from giant cells, the megakaryocytes.
When there is a wound they stick together and form a plug.
A platelet lives for only about a week.
Anyone with too few platelets bleeds more easily.

abschnitte.text: Platelets are even smaller than the **red blood cells**. They are tiny, flat discs without a **cell nucleus**. This is because they are not whole cells, but fragments of larger cells. Even so, millions of them float in a single drop of blood.

Like the other blood cells, platelets are made in the **bone marrow**. There live giant cells, the **megakaryocytes**. From each of these giant cells, thousands of small platelets pinch off and enter the blood. Because a platelet lives for only about **a week**, the body has to keep making new ones. A red blood cell, by contrast, lives for about four months.

When you cut yourself, the platelets rush to the injured spot. They stick to the wound and to each other. This makes a small **plug** that blocks the hole in the blood vessel like a cork. Then **blood clotting** begins: liquid blood becomes solid, and a scab forms.

If someone has **too few platelets**, bleeding stops less well. Such people also get **bruises** or nosebleeds more easily. If, on the other hand, the platelets stick together in the wrong place, a clot can block a vessel. Some medicines therefore make the platelets less sticky.

gewusst: Platelets can also be donated. This helps, for example, people who make too few of them themselves because of a serious illness.
Because they are constantly renewed, the body makes a huge number of new platelets every day.

teile.einleitung: Hypothermia means that the temperature inside the body falls below 35 degrees Celsius. This can happen in cold, wet and windy conditions, for example in the mountains or in cold water. That is why we dress warmly in winter, so that the body does not lose too much heat.
wichtigste: In hypothermia the core temperature falls below 35 degrees Celsius.
The technical term for it is hypothermia.
Wet and wind make the body cool down especially quickly.
Warm clothing stops the body from losing too much heat.
First signs are shivering, cold skin and tiredness.
Severe hypothermia is life-threatening and an emergency.
Children cool down faster than adults.

abschnitte.text: In **hypothermia** the body loses more heat than it can produce. Normally the core temperature is about 37 degrees. If it falls below 35 degrees, it is called **hypothermia**. To be distinguished from it is **frostbite**, in which only individual parts of the body such as fingers, toes or ears are damaged. Both can occur at the same time, however.

The body cools down fastest in **cold water**, because water conducts heat much better than air. Wet clothes and strong wind also draw away a lot of heat. At risk are mountaineers, winter sports fans or people after an avalanche accident. Children cool down faster because their bodies have more skin surface in proportion to their size. Older people are also especially at risk.

First you begin to **shiver** strongly, and the skin turns pale and cold. Hands and feet become stiff and clumsy. With further cooling the shivering stops, and the person becomes confused and drowsy. Heartbeat and breathing become slower. Below about 30 degrees you can lose consciousness, and the heart can get out of rhythm.

In winter the **layering method** helps: several layers of clothing on top of each other. Between the layers, warm air stays trapped, which insulates well. A hat is important, because a lot of heat is lost through the head. You should change wet clothes as quickly as possible. Warm drinks and enough food give the body energy for heating.

If you suspect severe hypothermia, in Switzerland you call the ambulance service on **144**, and in the mountains also Rega on 1414. You carefully bring the person to a warm place sheltered from the wind. Wet clothing is removed and the person wrapped in blankets or a **rescue blanket**. People who are severely chilled should not be rubbed hard or made to walk around. Otherwise cold blood from the arms and legs can flow to the heart and become dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for being dangerously cold, that is a core temperature below 35 degrees.
Damage by cold to individual parts of the body such as fingers or toes.
Several layers of clothing on top of each other that keep you warm.
A thin, shiny foil that holds in body heat.

gewusst: Water conducts heat about 25 times better than air, which is why you cool down so quickly in a cold lake.
Some people have survived severe hypothermia because their bodies needed less oxygen in the cold.
In rescues, experts often say that nobody is dead until they are warm and dead.

teile.einleitung: Non-specific defence is the part of the immune system that we are born with. It acts at once against many different germs without telling them apart exactly. It is the body's first line of defence.
wichtigste: Non-specific defence is also called innate immune defence.
It reacts quickly against many germs.
Healthy skin forms a tight barrier.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills many swallowed germs.
Lysozyme in tears and saliva attacks bacteria.
Natural killer cells kill cells infected by viruses.

abschnitte.text: A distinction is made between two parts of the defence. **Non-specific defence** is something you have from birth, so it is also called **innate immune defence**. It does not distinguish exactly between individual germs. But it reacts very quickly, within the first minutes to hours. **Specific defence**, on the other hand, is acquired only in the course of life. It is slower, but remembers individual germs precisely.

The first hurdle is the **skin**. Its horny layer cannot be penetrated by most germs. Only with injuries can they get in easily. The **mucous membranes** in the nose and mouth are covered with mucus, on which germs get stuck. In the stomach, **hydrochloric acid** kills many swallowed germs. In tears and saliva there is the enzyme **lysozyme**, which attacks the cell wall of bacteria. It was described in 1922 by **Alexander Fleming**.

On the skin and in the gut live countless harmless bacteria. This **bacterial flora** densely populates the surfaces. Harmful germs therefore find hardly any room and food to settle. So the useful bacteria are a kind of protective shield. That is why it is important for this flora to stay healthy.

If germs do get into the body, **scavenger cells** come into action. They surround bacteria and digest them. **Natural killer cells** recognise diseased body cells, for example ones infected by viruses, by changed features on their surface. They kill these cells without having to know the germ beforehand. At the site of a fight, an **inflammation** with redness and swelling often develops.

**Fever** is also part of the defence. Many germs multiply less well at a raised temperature. At the same time some defence reactions run faster. Fever is therefore often a sign that the body is fighting an illness. With a very high fever, or if it lasts a long time, however, you should ask a doctor.

gewusst: Alexander Fleming is said to have discovered lysozyme when a drop from his nose fell into a dish of bacteria.
Even sneezing and coughing are part of the defence: this is how the body flings out dust and germs.

teile.einleitung: Swiss Air Rescue, Rega for short, helps people in need from the air. With helicopters it quickly picks up the injured and sick, including from the mountains. Rega is a non-profit foundation.
wichtigste: Rega is the abbreviation for Schweizerische Rettungsflugwacht, Swiss Air Rescue.
With the helicopter it quickly fetches injured people from the mountains.
Its alarm number is 1414.
It was founded in 1952.
It is supported mainly by donor members.

abschnitte.text: **Rega** flies with red and white **rescue helicopters** to emergencies all over Switzerland. This is especially important in the **mountains**, where an ambulance cannot get to or only slowly. On board are a pilot, an emergency doctor and a rescue specialist. Often the helicopter can land right at the scene of the accident. If that is not possible, it lifts the injured up with a **rescue winch** on a cable.

Rega has its own **alarm number: 1414**. You can also alert it through an app that transmits the exact location. In emergencies you can also dial the emergency number 144. The operations centre then decides whether a helicopter, an ambulance or both come. The helicopters are spread over various bases in Switzerland so that they are quick everywhere.

Rega was founded in **1952**. It is a **non-profit foundation** and gets its money mainly from **donor members** who pay a contribution every year. A great many people in Switzerland support it in this way. Besides helicopters, Rega also has **ambulance jets**. With them it brings patients who fell ill or were injured abroad back to Switzerland.

gewusst: Rega also flies at night and in difficult weather when safety allows.
From abroad you can reach Rega on the number +41 333 333 333.

teile.einleitung: Tissue engineering means growing living tissue in the laboratory. Researchers make tissue that is meant to replace or repair diseased or injured tissue in the body. Some methods are already in use, but much of it is still research.
wichtigste: The aim is to make working tissue in the laboratory.
Cells, a supporting framework and growth factors are combined.
The supporting framework is called a scaffold.
The body's own cells prevent rejection reactions.
Grown skin has been used for large burns since the 1980s.
A great difficulty is supplying thick tissue with blood vessels.

abschnitte.text: Tissue engineering needs three things: living **cells**, a **supporting framework** and **growth factors** that give the cells signals. The framework is called a **scaffold**. It gives the cells a three-dimensional shape and often consists of degradable plastics or natural biomaterials. When the tissue has grown, the framework dissolves over time.

The best choice is to use the patient's **own cells**, which are called **autologous**. The immune system recognises them as its own and does not reject them. So no long-term medicines against rejection are needed. One example is **autologous chondrocyte transplantation**: healthy cartilage cells are taken from a part of the joint that is under little strain, multiplied in the laboratory and placed in a cartilage defect, for example in the knee.

One of the first successes was grown **skin**. Since the **1980s**, skin cells have been multiplied from a small skin sample in the laboratory to form thin layers. These can be transferred onto the wounds of people with extensive **burns**. Growing tissue is often kept in a **bioreactor**, which controls temperature, oxygen and nutrients.

In **3D bioprinting**, a machine prints “bio-inks” containing living cells layer by layer. In this way shapes such as cartilage or fine vessels can be built up. In **decellularisation**, all the cells are washed out of a donor organ with mild detergents. What is left is the framework, which can then be repopulated with the patient's cells.

Growing whole organs is still very difficult. By diffusion, oxygen travels only about **0.1 to 0.2 millimetres** from a blood vessel into the tissue. Thick tissue therefore needs a fine **network of blood vessels**, otherwise it dies inside. Many groups around the world are researching this, including at Swiss universities.

gewusst: A bioreactor can even move or stretch tissue so that, for example, it becomes as strong as real cartilage.
Many frameworks are built so that they dissolve by themselves in the body.

teile.einleitung: Thermoreceptors are sensory cells that detect warmth and cold. Most of them sit in our skin. Thanks to them we notice straight away whether the bath water is too hot or the wind is cold.
wichtigste: The skin has separate receptors for cold and for warmth.
Cold receptors are found in the skin much more often than warm receptors.
Menthol stimulates the cold receptors, which is why peppermint feels cool.
Thermoreceptors mainly report changes in temperature.
From about 45 °C you also feel pain.
The hypothalamus in the brain monitors the temperature of the blood.

abschnitte.text: The perception of warmth and cold is called **thermoception** in technical language. Two kinds of sensory cells are responsible: **cold receptors** and **warm receptors**. They are not found everywhere, but at individual **cold spots** and **warm spots**. If you probe the skin with a cold metal tip, you only feel the cold at certain places. There are many more cold spots than warm spots.

Hold one hand in cold water and the other in warm water. Then dip both into lukewarm water. The hand that was cold before feels it as **warm**, the hand that was warm before as **cool**. This shows that thermoreceptors mainly report the **change** compared with before. That is why a lake also feels cold at first and more pleasant after a few minutes.

Some substances can fool thermoreceptors. **Menthol** from peppermint activates a cold receptor without it actually getting colder. The brain then reports “cool”. In the opposite way, the hot substance **capsaicin** from chilli stimulates a receptor for heat. That is why spicy food burns like fire in the mouth.

If it gets very hot, from about **45 °C**, **pain sensors** also react. The burning feeling warns us of a scald, and we pull our hand back in a flash. There are also temperature-sensitive nerve cells inside the body. In the **hypothalamus** they measure the temperature of the blood and, when needed, set off sweating or shivering.

gewusst: Pit vipers have pit organs between the eye and the nostril, with which they can sense the body heat of their prey even in the dark.
Because cold receptors are more common, we notice cooling especially quickly.

teile.einleitung: Tears do not flow only when we cry. A fine film of tears covers our eyes all the time. It keeps them moist and clean and protects them from germs.
wichtigste: Tears consist for the most part of water.
They are made in the lacrimal gland at the top outer side above the eye.
The tear film keeps the eye moist and washes dust away.
Substances in the tears harm bacteria.
A duct leads tears from the inner corner of the eye into the nose.
We blink about 10 to 15 times a minute.

abschnitte.text: Tears are for the most part **water**. In addition there are small amounts of **salt** and other substances. That is why tears taste slightly salty. Among the substances is the enzyme **lysozyme**. It attacks the cell wall of bacteria and so helps to kill germs. So tears protect the eye from infections.

The **lacrimal gland** lies at the top outer edge of the eye socket, under the bone above the eye. It constantly makes a little tear fluid. With every **blink**, the eyelid spreads it over the eye like a windscreen wiper. A person blinks about 10 to 15 times a minute, mostly without noticing. A blink lasts only a fraction of a second.

At the **inner corner of the eye** there are small openings. From there a fine duct, the **nasolacrimal duct**, leads into the nose. There the tear fluid drains away. If you cry hard, so many tears come that your nose runs too. That is why when you cry you often need a tissue for both eyes and nose straight away.

In many **newborn babies**, hardly any tears come yet when they cry. In the first weeks they often still make little tear fluid. In adults the eyes can sometimes be too dry, for example after working at a screen for a long time, because you blink less then. Then **artificial tears** as eye drops help. They moisten the eye.

gewusst: Onions make us cry because cutting them releases a substance that irritates the eyes.
Lysozyme in tears was discovered by the researcher Alexander Fleming, who later also found penicillin.

teile.einleitung: In a thrombosis, a blood clot forms in a blood vessel. It can partly or completely block the vessel. Most often this affects the deep veins in the legs.
wichtigste: A thrombosis is a blood clot that blocks a blood vessel.
The clot is called a thrombus.
Thromboses most often form in the deep leg veins.
A dangerous consequence is a pulmonary embolism.
Sitting for a long time, for example on a long-haul flight, raises the risk.
It is treated with anticoagulants, and movement and compression stockings help to prevent it.

abschnitte.text: The clot in a thrombosis is called a **thrombus**. It consists mainly of **platelets**, **fibrin** and trapped blood cells. With a wound, clotting is useful, because it stops the bleeding. In a thrombosis, however, the clot forms inside a vessel and obstructs the flow of blood.

In the **deep leg veins** the blood flows slowly and against gravity to the heart. The **calf muscles** help like a pump. If you sit still for hours, for example on a **long-haul flight**, this pump hardly works. Other risks are bed rest after operations, injuries, smoking and certain illnesses. The doctor Rudolf Virchow described three causes: slow blood flow, a damaged vessel wall and a changed make-up of the blood.

If the blood backs up behind the clot, the **leg swells**. It often feels **warm** and tight and **hurts**, especially in the calf. Sometimes the skin turns slightly bluish. With such signs you should see a doctor quickly, because a thrombosis can be detected well with ultrasound.

If a clot comes loose, it can be swept with the blood through the heart into the lung. There it blocks a vessel. This is called a **pulmonary embolism**, and it can be life-threatening. Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain is an emergency, and then in Switzerland you dial **144**.

For treatment there are **anticoagulants**, often called blood thinners. They stop the clot from growing, and the body can slowly dissolve it. For prevention, **compression stockings** help: they press on the legs so that the blood flows back to the heart faster. On long journeys you should also get up, walk around, move your feet and drink enough.

gewusst: Clots can also form in arteries. They are a common cause of heart attack and stroke.
Even simply rocking your feet while sitting gets the calf pump going.

teile.einleitung: UV-B radiation is a high-energy part of sunlight. It is the main cause of sunburn and can directly damage the genetic material of skin cells. At the same time the skin needs UV-B to make vitamin D.
wichtigste: UV-B ranges from 280 to 315 nanometres.
UV-B mainly causes sunburn.
It is absorbed directly by DNA and forms pyrimidine dimers.
Repeated exposure thickens the horny layer.
The redness is strongest about 12 to 24 hours after exposure.
The UV index weights UV-B especially strongly.

abschnitte.text: UV-B lies between UV-C and UV-A and ranges from **280 to 315 nanometres**. The shorter the wavelength, the more energy a single **photon**, that is a particle of light, carries. That is why a UV-B photon has more energy than a UV-A photon. A large part of UV-B is held back by the **ozone layer**, but not all of it. UV-B is strongly absorbed in the outer skin, the **epidermis**.

UV-B sets off an inflammation in the skin: **sunburn**. Messenger substances gradually widen the blood vessels, and the skin turns red and hot. The redness begins after a few hours and is usually strongest **12 to 24 hours** after exposure. That is why you often only notice sunburn in the evening. Repeated exposure thickens the **horny layer**. This **light callus** holds back part of the radiation.

DNA absorbs UV-B directly. In the process neighbouring building blocks, the **pyrimidine bases** such as thymine, join into **pyrimidine dimers**. When the DNA is copied, **mutations** can result. It is typical that a cytosine is replaced by a thymine. This “UV signature” reveals that a tumour was caused by UV radiation. Especially often affected is the gene **TP53**, which normally stops cell division when there is damage.

How strongly the sun endangers the skin is shown by the **UV index**. For it, the radiation is weighted by its sunburn effect, the so-called erythemal action spectrum. UV-B counts especially strongly in it. One index level corresponds to **25 milliwatts** of sunburn-causing radiation per square metre. In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss publishes values and forecasts every day.

UV-B also has a useful side. With its help the skin makes **vitamin D**, which is important for strong bones. For this a short time outdoors is enough. Ordinary **window glass** largely holds back UV-B. Behind a pane you therefore hardly get sunburn, but also hardly make any vitamin D.

gewusst: You cannot feel UV-B: the warmth of the sun comes from other radiation. That is why you do not notice how strong the UV radiation is at the moment.
On snow in the mountains a large part of the UV radiation is thrown back, which is why you easily get sunburn when skiing.

teile.einleitung: Sweat glands are tiny glands in the skin that make sweat. They make sure that the body does not overheat. A person has several million of them.
wichtigste: Sweating serves mainly to cool the body.
There are especially many sweat glands on the palms and soles.
On a normal day without sport, you sweat about half a litre.
In sport in great heat, you can lose more than a litre an hour.
Well-trained athletes usually begin to sweat earlier.
Excessively strong sweating is called hyperhidrosis.

abschnitte.text: A **sweat gland** is a tiny, coiled tube deep in the skin. There the sweat is made, which flows through a fine duct to the **pore** at the skin’s surface. Almost everywhere on the body there are such glands. Especially many sit on the **palms** and **soles**. Fresh sweat smells **almost of nothing**. The typical smell arises only later through bacteria.

Sweating serves mainly to **cool the body**. The sweat evaporates on the skin and takes heat with it. On a normal day without sport, you sweat about **half a litre**, often without noticing. You also sweat a little **in your sleep**. In sport in great heat it can be **more than a litre an hour**. Because sweat contains salt, **white salt marks** are often left on a dried T-shirt.

You might think that athletes sweat less. The opposite is the case: **well-trained** people usually start to sweat **earlier** and often sweat more. Their body has learned to switch on the cooling quickly. So they overheat less easily and can keep going longer.

Not all animals cool themselves by sweating. The **pig** has hardly any sweat glands. That is why it likes to wallow in **mud**, which cools as it dries and protects from the sun. In humans there is also the opposite: some people sweat very strongly without it being hot or without exerting themselves. This is called **hyperhidrosis**. A doctor can help with it.

gewusst: Dogs have sweat glands mainly on the pads of their paws.
That hands become moist when you are excited is due to the many sweat glands on the palms.

teile.einleitung: Synaesthesia is a special way of perceiving the world. One stimulus also sets off an impression in another sense. Some people, for example, see colours when they hear music.
wichtigste: In synaesthesia, sense impressions are linked together.
The Greek word means roughly feeling together.
A common form is grapheme-colour synaesthesia.
A few per cent of people have some form of it.
Synaesthesia is not regarded as an illness.
The links usually stay the same for years.

abschnitte.text: In **synaesthesia** two senses are connected with each other. A sound can set off a colour, a word a taste. The word is made up of the Greek “syn” for together and “aisthesis” for sensation. So it means **feeling together**. What is meant is the shared sensing of several senses.

A common form is **grapheme-colour synaesthesia**. A **grapheme** is a written character. People with it might, for example, always see the letter A as red or the number 7 as green. These links stay the **same** for many years. Someone who sees the 5 as blue will still see it as blue years later. Researchers use this consistency as a test for genuine synaesthesia.

Studies estimate that **a few per cent** of people have synaesthetic perceptions. Many do not even know that this is something special, because for them it has always been that way. Synaesthesia runs in some families. So it is thought that **genes** play a part. Today synaesthesia is regarded as a special way of perceiving, **not as an illness**, and it needs no treatment.

The painter **Wassily Kandinsky** is often linked with synaesthesia. He described experiencing sounds as colours, and he translated music into colours and shapes. Many of his abstract paintings have titles from music, such as “Composition” or “Improvisation”. Many people with synaesthesia find their perception to be an enrichment.

gewusst: Two people with synaesthesia usually see the same letter in quite different colours.
Some people with synaesthesia can remember numbers especially well thanks to their colours.

teile.einleitung: When we are hot or exert ourselves, the skin becomes moist: we sweat. Sweat is the body’s built-in cooling. It consists mainly of water and tastes salty.
wichtigste: Sweat consists mainly of water.
It tastes salty because it contains salt.
It is made in small sweat glands in the skin.
It comes out through tiny pores.
Sweat cools by evaporating on the skin.
It smells unpleasant only because of bacteria on the skin.
Anyone who sweats a lot must drink enough water.

abschnitte.text: Sweat consists almost entirely of **water**. In it, small amounts of **salt** are dissolved, mainly table salt. That is why **sweat tastes salty**. Traces of other substances are added. Sweat is made in tiny **sweat glands** in the skin. Through fine channels it reaches the **pores**, small openings on the surface of the skin.

Our body works best at a temperature of around 37 degrees. If it gets too warm, we start to sweat. The sweat **evaporates** on the skin, that is, it turns into water vapour. For this it needs heat, and it takes this from the skin. In this way the body **cools** down. You know this too when you come out of the water wet and freeze in the wind.

You sweat most with **exertion on hot days**, for example when running in the sun. Many people sweat especially strongly **under the armpits**, but also on the forehead, back, hands and feet. Sometimes you also sweat from excitement or fear, for example before an exam. Anyone who sweats a lot loses water and salt. That is why it is important to **drink enough water** during sport.

Fresh sweat hardly smells. On the skin, though, many tiny **bacteria** live. They break down substances in the sweat, and smells arise in the process. That is why **sweat smells unpleasant after a while**. Regular washing and fresh clothes help against it. Many people also use a deodorant.

gewusst: A person has several million sweat glands.
Humans are among the living things that can cool themselves best by sweating.

teile.einleitung: UV-A radiation is the longest-wavelength part of the sun's ultraviolet radiation. It is invisible, penetrates deep into the skin and makes up the largest part of the UV radiation at ground level. Above all, it makes the skin age too early.
wichtigste: UV-A ranges from 315 to 400 nanometres in wavelength.
About 95 per cent of UV radiation at ground level is UV-A.
UV-A penetrates as far as the dermis.
It mainly causes premature skin ageing.
Ordinary window glass lets a lot of UV-A through.
Sunbeds tan mainly with UV-A.

abschnitte.text: Light and UV radiation consist of waves. UV-A covers wavelengths of **315 to 400 nanometres** and borders on visible violet. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. The **ozone layer** strongly filters short-wavelength UV radiation, but hardly filters the long-wavelength UV-A. That is why UV radiation at ground level consists of **about 95 per cent** UV-A.

Because of its longer wavelength, UV-A gets deeper into the skin than UV-B. It reaches the **dermis**. There it damages **collagen** and **elastic fibres**, which give the skin firmness. In the long run wrinkles and leathery skin develop. This **photoageing** is the typical effect of UV-A. UV-A, by contrast, causes sunburn much less.

DNA, the genetic material in the cells, absorbs UV-A only weakly. But UV-A produces **free radicals** and other **reactive oxygen compounds**. These are very reactive particles that damage the genetic material indirectly. This is called **oxidative damage**. In the long run it can contribute to the development of skin cancer.

abschnitte.titel: Behind glass and in the sunbed
abschnitte.text: Ordinary **window glass** largely holds back UV-B, but lets a large part of the UV-A radiation through. Behind glass you therefore hardly get sunburn, but the skin can still age. The lamps of most **sunbeds** tan mainly with UV-A, often with some UV-B. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classes the use of sunbeds as **carcinogenic**. In Switzerland minors are not allowed to use a sunbed.

A good sun protection must also protect against UV-A, not just against sunburn. In the EU there is a **circled UVA logo** for this. It may appear only on products whose UV-A protection reaches at least a third of the stated **sun protection factor**. In addition, clothes, a hat, sunglasses and shade over midday protect you.

gewusst: Some insects such as bees can see UV-A. Many flowers have patterns that are visible only in UV light.
UV-A lamps make certain substances glow. This is used, for example, to check the security features on banknotes.

teile.einleitung: The UV index is a simple number that shows how strong the sun's UV radiation is at the moment. The higher the number, the faster you get sunburn. This way you know how well you need to protect yourself.
wichtigste: The UV index shows the strength of the UV radiation.
From a value of 3 you should protect yourself.
At midday the UV index is highest.
In the lowlands it is highest in summer.
Values from 11 are considered extreme.
You can find the UV index in the weather forecast.

abschnitte.text: The **UV index** is a number for the strength of UV radiation. It starts at 0 and can rise above 11. Values from 1 to 2 count as **low**, 3 to 5 as **moderate**, 6 to 7 as **high**, 8 to 10 as **very high**. From 11 the radiation is **extreme**. Then unprotected skin burns very quickly. The same scale is used all over the world.

From a UV index of **3** sun protection is recommended. Then a **hat**, **clothes** with sleeves, **sunglasses** and **sun cream** are part of it. At a high value it is best to seek **shade** at midday. Below 3 the radiation is low, and you usually need no special protection.

Around **midday** the sun is at its highest. Then the path of the rays through the air is shortest, and the UV index is greatest. In **summer** the sun stands especially high at midday, so the value in the lowlands is then highest. In the morning, in the evening and in winter it is usually much lower.

Many **weather forecasts** and weather apps show the UV index for today and tomorrow. In Switzerland it is published by **MeteoSwiss**. In the **mountains** the UV index is higher than in the lowlands, because the layer of air above is thinner. On **snow** a lot of radiation is also thrown back. That is why you need sun protection even when skiing in winter.

gewusst: The UV index can also be high on cloudy days, because part of the radiation comes through the clouds.
At the equator the UV index is often very high all year round, because the sun stands almost straight overhead there.

teile.einleitung: The eardrum is a thin membrane deep in the ear. It catches sound and passes it on so that we can hear. Because it is so delicate, you have to protect it well.
wichtigste: The eardrum sits at the end of the ear canal.
It separates the ear canal from the middle ear.
Sound makes the eardrum vibrate.
Behind it lie the hammer, anvil and stirrup.
A very loud bang can make the eardrum burst.
Small holes often heal up again by themselves.

abschnitte.titel: A skin like on a drum
abschnitte.text: A drum has a stretched skin on top, the **drumhead**. The eardrum in the ear is stretched in a similar way and can vibrate. It is only about a centimetre across and very thin. It sits at the end of the **ear canal** and separates it from the **middle ear**. You cannot see it from outside, only the doctor with a special instrument with a light.

Sound consists of fine vibrations of the air. These vibrations travel through the ear canal to the eardrum and make it tremble. Behind the eardrum lie three tiny bones, the **ossicles**: the **hammer**, the **anvil** and the **stirrup**. They pass the vibrations on to the inner ear. There they are converted into signals for the brain.

When a plane lands or when you drive quickly up into the mountains, the **air pressure** changes. Then the air presses more strongly on one side of the eardrum, and the ear feels blocked. A fine passage, the **Eustachian tube**, connects the middle ear with the throat. When you **swallow** or **chew gum**, it opens briefly, air flows in, and the pressure evens out.

A very loud **bang** can injure the eardrum so that it gets a small hole. A loud scream right at the ear can also hurt and damage hearing. That is why you never shout in someone's ear. On 1 August (Swiss National Day) or on New Year's Eve, ear protection helps when fireworks go off. Cotton buds also do not belong deep in the ear canal.

A small hole in the eardrum can often **heal up** by itself within a few weeks. Even so, a doctor should look at the ear. The specialist responsible is the **ear, nose and throat doctor**, ENT doctor for short. Ears, nose and throat are connected on the inside, so he looks after all three. If there is pain or poor hearing, you should not wait too long.

gewusst: The stirrup behind the eardrum is the smallest bone of the human body.
The three ossicles are named after tools and objects because they resemble them in shape.

teile.einleitung: Toilet hygiene means using the toilet in such a way that it stays clean and no germs are passed on. With a few simple habits you protect yourself and everyone who comes after you.
wichtigste: After using the toilet you flush.
Before flushing you close the lid, so that fewer splashes get into the air.
Wet wipes belong in the rubbish bin, not in the WC.
You clean the bowl with the toilet brush.
If the paper is almost used up, you put out a new roll.
It is better to leave your phone outside, so that no germs get on it.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland people mostly say **WC** for the toilet, which stands for “water closet”. After using it you press the **flush**, so that the toilet is clean for the next person. When flushing, fine droplets spray upwards. A **closed lid** holds them back. If the bowl is dirty, you scrub it with the **toilet brush**, which stands next to the toilet.

**Wet wipes** do not dissolve in water and block the pipes. So you put them in the **rubbish bin**. Only toilet paper belongs in the WC. If the roll is almost empty, you put out a **new roll** so that the next person also has enough paper. If there is no roll, you tell a grown-up.

After the WC you wash your hands thoroughly with **soap** at the **“Lavabo”**, which is what the washbasin is called in Switzerland. In public toilets you often dry your hands with **paper towels** or a **hand dryer** that blows warm air. This keeps your hands clean so that they do not pass on germs.

In the toilet, **germs** easily get onto the phone. Later you touch it again and hold it to your face. So it is better not to take it with you to the WC. Anyone who has it with them anyway should clean it now and then.

gewusst: A closed toilet lid clearly reduces the droplets in the air when flushing.
Phones are among the objects we touch most often, and so they carry many germs.

teile.einleitung: A tumour is a swelling or growth in the body that arises when cells multiply without control. There are benign and malignant tumours. Malignant tumours are also called cancer.
wichtigste: A tumour arises when cells grow without control.
Benign tumours push tissue aside, malignant ones grow into it destructively.
A sarcoma arises from bone, cartilage or muscles.
An adenoma is a benign tumour of glandular tissue.
A biopsy shows for certain whether a tumour is benign or malignant.
The TNM system describes how far a tumour has spread.

abschnitte.text: Normally cells divide only when the body needs new ones. In a **tumour**, cells get out of control and keep on growing. **Benign tumours** grow slowly and only push the tissue aside. **Malignant tumours** grow **invasively**: they break through tissue boundaries and destroy the tissue around them. They can also form daughter growths in other organs, the **metastases**.

Tumours are named after the tissue they arise from. A **sarcoma** is a malignant tumour of connective or supporting tissue, for example of bone, cartilage, muscle or fat. Sarcomas are much rarer than tumours of covering tissue. An **adenoma** is a benign tumour of glandular tissue, for example a polyp in the large intestine. Some adenomas can become malignant over time.

From a size of a few millimetres, a tumour needs its own **blood vessels** to get oxygen and nutrients. The formation of new vessels is called **angiogenesis**. The tumour sends out signalling substances for this, such as VEGF. Healthy cells with damage to their genetic material normally die in a controlled way. This programmed cell death is called **apoptosis**. Cancer cells often switch it off and survive despite the damage.

**Malignant melanoma** is a malignant skin cancer. It arises from the **pigment cells** of the skin, the melanocytes, which make the brown skin pigment. Strong UV radiation and sunburn raise the risk. Compared with the rest of Europe, Switzerland has many cases. That is why sun protection with clothes, a hat and sun cream is especially important.

In a **biopsy**, a small piece of tissue is taken and examined under the microscope. Only this tells you for certain whether a tumour is benign or malignant. With the **TNM classification**, the spread is described: T stands for the original tumour, N for affected lymph nodes and M for metastases. Depending on the case, treatment is by **surgery**, **radiotherapy** or medicines such as **chemotherapy**.

gewusst: The word “tumour” comes from Latin and simply means “swelling”.
Many tumours are now discovered early and can be treated well. In Switzerland the Swiss Cancer League supports people affected and their families.

teile.einleitung: Sweets such as chocolate (known as “Schoggi” in Swiss German), boiled sweets or biscuits taste delicious and bring joy. But they contain a lot of sugar. So the rule is: enjoy them, but in small amounts, and brush your teeth afterwards.
wichtigste: Sweets contain a lot of sugar.
In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet.
The food pyramid recommends at most one small portion of sweet things a day.
You should brush your teeth after sweets.
Bees make honey from nectar.
“Schoggi” is the Swiss German word for chocolate.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss food pyramid** shows how much of which foods you should eat. At the bottom are drinks, vegetables and fruit, of which you need plenty. **Sweet things** are at the narrow **tip**. You may enjoy them, but only a small portion a day. After sweets you should **brush your teeth**, so that no sugar is left behind and no tooth decay develops.

In Switzerland sugar is made from **sugar beet**. The beets grow in fields on the Central Plateau and are processed in the sugar factories in **Aarberg** and **Frauenfeld**. A natural sweet food is **honey**. Bees collect nectar from flowers and make it into honey, which contains a lot of sugar.

Switzerland is famous for its **“Schoggi”**, which is what people say in Swiss German for chocolate. Boiled sweets are called **“Zältli”** and biscuits **“Guetzli”**. From Basel come the **Basler Läckerli**, small, hard gingerbread biscuits with honey and spices. **Meringues** are white, airy bakes made from whisked egg white and sugar. They are especially well known in the Bernese Oberland, where people like to eat them with cream.

If you fancy something sweet, you can also reach for **fruit**. It contains natural sugar, but also vitamins and fibre. Dried fruit such as dates or apricots is also sweet, but sticks to the teeth. It is best to eat sweets after a meal and not all day long.

gewusst: The village of Meiringen in the Bernese Oberland is often named as the home of meringues.
Switzerland is one of the countries where the most chocolate per person is eaten.

teile.einleitung: With **soap** we wash hands, body and laundry. It loosens grease and dirt so that water can rinse them away. People have been making soap for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Soap loosens grease and dirt from the skin.
Soap arises when you boil fat or oil with lye.
Rubbed with water, soap makes lather.
Curd soap is a simple, solid soap without fragrances.
Liquid soap comes from a dispenser with a pump.
A bar of soap should dry in a soap dish.

abschnitte.text: Water alone cannot dissolve grease well. Grease and water do not like each other and stay separate. Soap helps here like a **go-between**. One part of a soap particle holds on to the grease, the other to the water. In this way the grease is packed into small droplets and can be **rinsed away** with water.

If you rub soap with water, **lather** arises. It consists of many small bubbles. The lather spreads the soap well over the skin. For cleaning, though, what matters is mainly the soap itself, not the amount of lather. Thorough hand washing takes about 20 to 30 seconds.

For a long time, soap has been made from **fat and lye**. If you boil fat or oil with a lye, it turns into soap. This process is called **saponification**. In the past, animal fats and lye from wood ash were used for it. Today plant oils such as olive oil or coconut oil are often used.

**Curd soap** is a simple, solid soap without perfume. In the past it was used to wash hands, body and also the **laundry**. Today there are many soaps with scent and colour. **Liquid soap** comes from a bottle with a pump. You simply press the dispenser and at once have the right amount.

With every wash, a little soap dissolves in the water. That is why a bar becomes **smaller and smaller** over time. After use, it is best to put it in a **soap dish**, where it can drain and dry. If the soap lies in water, it becomes soft and slimy. This way a bar lasts much longer.

gewusst: Regular hand washing with soap is one of the most important ways to protect yourself from diseases.
In Aleppo in Syria, a well-known soap made from olive oil and laurel oil has been made for centuries.

teile.einleitung: UV filters are the active ingredients in sun creams that protect the skin from ultraviolet radiation. There are mineral and organic filters, and they work in different ways. The sun protection factor shows how strongly a cream protects.
wichtigste: Mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide scatter, reflect and absorb UV.
Organic filters absorb UV and give off the energy as heat.
The sun protection factor compares the sunburn threshold with and without protection.
SPF 30 holds back about 97 per cent of UV-B radiation.
In the laboratory 2 milligrams per square centimetre are applied.
Reapplying keeps up the protection but does not extend it.

abschnitte.text: **Mineral filters** are fine particles, above all **zinc oxide** and **titanium dioxide**. They throw UV radiation back, scatter it and partly absorb it. They are considered well tolerated, but can leave a **white film**. Large particles also scatter visible light. That is why titanium dioxide is often used as **nanoparticles**. Very small particles are almost transparent but still filter UV.

**Organic filters** are molecules that absorb UV photons, that is, take them in. In doing so they enter an **excited state**, a state with more energy. When they fall back, they give off the energy mainly as **heat**. This way the radiation does not reach the skin cells. Good sun creams combine several filters so that they protect against UV-B and UV-A.

The **sun protection factor**, SPF for short, compares the amount of UV that causes slight redness with sun protection to the amount without protection. SPF 20 means that about twenty times more radiation is needed. With **SPF 30** roughly one thirtieth reaches the skin, so about **97 per cent** is intercepted. It is measured with **2 milligrams per square centimetre**. In everyday life most people use much less, and the protection falls.

**Reapplying** replaces cream that has been rubbed or washed off. It does not, however, extend the total protection time. That comes from the skin's own **natural protection time** and the SPF. In the EU **“50+”** is the highest value allowed. Higher numbers would suggest extra performance that hardly exists.

Some organic filters are suspected of harming **corals**. The US state of **Hawaii** therefore decided in 2018, as the first, to ban the sale of sun protection products with **oxybenzone** and **octinoxate**. It came into force in 2021. Whatever the case, clothes, a hat and shade protect reliably and do not end up in the water.

gewusst: An SPF 50 sun protection holds back only a little more UV-B than an SPF 30, namely about 98 instead of 97 per cent.
For the whole body of an adult you need about as much sun cream as fits into a small shot glass.

teile.einleitung: Psoriasis is a skin disease in which reddened, scaly patches appear. It is not contagious and can be treated well today, but usually not cured completely.
wichtigste: The technical term for the disease is psoriasis.
Psoriasis is not contagious.
The immune system wrongly triggers an inflammation in the skin.
The epidermis renews itself far too fast.
Typical are reddened patches with silvery-white scales on the elbows, knees and scalp.
Fingernails and joints can also be affected.
One treatment is UV light therapy.

abschnitte.titel: The immune system makes a mistake
abschnitte.text: The **immune system** normally protects the body from disease-causing agents. In **psoriasis**, though, it wrongly triggers an **inflammation** in the skin. So it is not an infection, and you **cannot catch it** from others. Often psoriasis runs in families. Stress, infections or certain medicines can trigger a new flare-up.

The top layer of skin is called the **epidermis**. It renews itself constantly: new cells grow up from below, old cells fall off at the top as fine flakes. Normally this takes about four weeks. In psoriasis it goes **much too fast**, often in a few days. The cells pile up and form thick, **silvery-white scales** on reddened skin.

Especially often affected are the **elbows**, the **knees** and the **scalp**. The patches have sharp edges and can itch. The **fingernails** often change too: they get small **pits** that look like pinpricks. In some people, **joints** also become inflamed, ache and swell. This is then called psoriatic arthritis.

Psoriasis usually cannot be cured completely, but it can be treated well. Ointments and creams loosen the scales and calm the inflammation. In **UV light therapy**, the skin is irradiated in a targeted way with ultraviolet light. For severe forms there are medicines that slow down the immune system. A skin specialist works with those affected to find the right treatment.

gewusst: Many people with psoriasis notice that their skin gets better in summer with more sun.
The word psoriasis comes from Greek and has to do with itching.

teile.einleitung: Systole is the phase of the heartbeat in which the ventricles contract and pump blood into the body. It is followed by diastole, in which the heart relaxes and fills up again.
wichtigste: Systole means contraction in Greek.
In systole the ventricles pump blood into the large arteries.
It begins with the tensing phase, followed by the ejection phase.
During ejection the aortic and pulmonary valves are open.
At the start of systole you hear the first heart sound.
In systole the pressure in the aorta is at its highest.

abschnitte.text: The word **systole** comes from Greek and means **contraction**. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase. The muscle of the **ventricles** contracts and presses the blood into the large arteries: the left ventricle into the **aorta**, the right into the pulmonary artery. This is followed by **diastole**, in which the muscle relaxes and the ventricles fill up again.

Heart valves work like valves in a pipe and make sure that blood flows in one direction only. During ejection the **semilunar valves** at the exits of the ventricles open, that is the **aortic and pulmonary valves**. The **atrioventricular valves** to the atria are closed so that no blood flows back.

At the start the ventricle muscle tenses, but all the valves are briefly closed. In this **tensing phase** no blood flows out yet, only the pressure rises. As soon as the pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the artery, the valve opens. Now the **ejection phase** begins, and the blood streams out.

At the start of systole the atrioventricular valves close and the heart muscle tenses. This produces the **first heart sound**, which you hear with a stethoscope. When the left ventricle ejects blood, the pressure in the aorta rises to its peak. This **systolic blood pressure** is the first, higher number when blood pressure is measured. An **extrasystole** is an additional, premature heartbeat. Occasional extrasystoles are common and usually harmless.

gewusst: With a blood pressure of 120 over 80, 120 is the systolic value.
The second heart sound is produced when the semilunar valves close at the end of systole.

teile.einleitung: Sweating is the way our body cools itself in heat and exertion. Not all living things do it the same way: dogs pant, horses sweat heavily. With a few tricks you also get through hot days well.
wichtigste: A dog hardly sweats and cools itself by panting with its mouth open.
Horses sweat heavily when they gallop fast.
Light, airy clothes are pleasant when sweating in summer.
Anyone who stays in the shade sweats less.
On muggy days sweat hardly dries, which is why you feel sticky.
Against sweat smell, many people use a deodorant.

abschnitte.text: If the body gets too warm, it sends **sweat** onto the skin. When the sweat **evaporates**, it takes heat with it and cools the skin. This keeps body temperature about the same. You sweat in heat, in sport, in fever and sometimes also from excitement. Because you lose water in the process, you have to drink enough.

On **muggy days** the air is very damp. Then it can hardly take up any more water. The **sweat hardly dries** and stays on the skin. That is why you feel **sticky** and are hot despite sweating. In dry heat, on the other hand, sweat evaporates quickly, and you often do not notice at all how much you are sweating.

A **dog** hardly sweats, only a little on the paws. It cools itself by **panting with its mouth open**. In the process, moisture evaporates from the tongue and airways. The **horse**, on the other hand, sweats heavily, especially when it **gallops** fast. Often you then see white foam on its coat. Cats groom themselves and spread saliva over their fur, which cools as it dries.

Anyone who **stays in the shade** sweats less. **Light, airy clothes**, for example of cotton or linen, let the skin breathe. At midday, when the sun is strongest, it is better to avoid great exertion. Against **sweat smell**, regular washing helps. Many people also use a **deodorant** under the armpits.

gewusst: A horse can lose many litres of sweat with great exertion.
Pigs hardly sweat and prefer to cool themselves in a mud puddle.

teile.einleitung: You need a handkerchief to blow your nose, above all when you have a cold. In Switzerland people often call it a “Nastuch”. Used properly, it helps to stop germs from being passed on.
wichtigste: In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a “Nastuch”.
Disposable tissues are made of soft paper.
You use a paper tissue only once.
You blow one nostril after the other.
After blowing your nose you wash your hands.
Used tissues contain germs.

abschnitte.text: It is best to blow **one nostril after the other**. You hold one nostril closed and blow gently through the other. That way you do not push the mucus into your ears. With a **cold** your nose often runs, and then you need a lot of tissues. Afterwards you **wash your hands**, because germs get onto your fingers when you blow your nose.

**Disposable tissues** are made of soft, absorbent paper. That is why they are also called **paper handkerchiefs**. They are meant for **single use**. For the next time you take a fresh one and throw the old one in the bin. In the past, people mainly used handkerchiefs made of **cloth**, which are washed again and again. In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a **“Nastuch”**.

There can be **viruses** and **bacteria** in nasal mucus. That is why you do not touch other people's used tissues, otherwise you can catch something. If you do not have a tissue to hand, it is best to sneeze or cough into the **crook of your elbow** instead of into your hand. That way fewer germs end up on door handles or toys.

To have fresh tissues with you when you are out and about, you put a small **pack** in your pocket or school bag. The pack keeps the tissues clean and dry. You can take it anywhere, to school, on trips or to training.

gewusst: A used paper tissue belongs in the rubbish bin, not in the waste paper.
When you sneeze, the air can shoot out of the nose and mouth at great speed.

teile.einleitung: A tattoo is a picture or pattern that is pricked into the skin with ink so that it lasts for good. People have been tattooing themselves for thousands of years. Because the skin is injured in the process, a fresh tattoo needs care.
wichtigste: The ink is pricked into the dermis.
Scavenger cells take up the ink and hold on to it.
Ötzi has more than 60 tattoos.
The word tattoo comes from Polynesia.
Among the Māori, face tattoos have a long tradition.
Tattoos are usually removed with a laser.

abschnitte.text: When tattooing, a fine needle pricks the skin very many times and brings ink in as it does so. The ink has to reach the **dermis**, the layer under the outer skin. If it lay only in the **epidermis**, it would flake off after a few weeks, because this layer constantly renews itself. In the dermis, **scavenger cells**, also called macrophages, take up the particles of ink. Because they cannot break them down, the picture stays visible.

The glacier mummy **Ötzi** from the Ötztal Alps is over 5,000 years old. More than 60 tattoos made of lines and crosses were found on his skin. The word “tattoo” goes back to **“tatau”** from Tahiti in Polynesia. Sailors around **James Cook** brought it to Europe in the 18th century. Among the **Māori** in New Zealand the traditional tattoos are called **Tā moko**. They show a person's origin and standing.

In tattooing the skin is injured thousands of times. A fresh tattoo is therefore a **wound** that first has to heal. Until then you should not go swimming and should not expose the tattoo to the sun. Germs in the water can cause infections, and sunlight can damage the ink. Later on, too, sun cream protects the tattoo from fading.

A **henna tattoo** is a painted design that disappears after a while. Henna only stains the upper layers of the skin and fades after a few weeks. There are warnings about so-called “black henna” with added substances, because it can cause allergies. A real tattoo is today usually removed with a **laser**. The light breaks up the particles of ink, which the body then gradually clears away. This usually takes several sessions.

gewusst: Ötzi's tattoos are often on joints and on the back. Researchers suspect that they may have been used to treat pain.
Removing a tattoo usually takes much longer and costs more than getting it.

teile.einleitung: A syncope is a brief faint. You lose consciousness for a few seconds because the brain briefly gets too little blood, and you usually recover quickly afterwards.
wichtigste: Syncope is the technical term for a brief faint.
The cause is a short reduction of blood flow to the brain.
A faint usually lasts only seconds to a few minutes.
Standing for a long time in great heat can bring on a faint.
Your vision going black is a typical warning sign.
You lay the person flat and raise their legs.

abschnitte.text: In a **syncope**, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen, and you lose consciousness for a moment. The term comes from Greek. Typically you come round again by yourself after seconds or a few minutes. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.

A faint happens especially easily when **standing for a long time in great heat**. The blood vessels widen, and blood collects in the legs. Some people faint at the sight of blood or when they are in pain. In this **vasovagal syncope** the nervous system reacts too strongly, and pulse and blood pressure suddenly drop.

Before a faint, **dizziness**, **blackouts of vision**, nausea and sweating often appear. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away. That way you can avoid a fall. It also helps to drink enough and to move your leg muscles when standing for a long time.

If someone has fainted briefly and is breathing normally, you lay the person **flat** and **raise their legs**. This lets more blood flow to the heart and the brain, and usually the person comes round quickly. If the person stays unconscious but breathes normally, you put them in the **recovery position**. This keeps the airways clear. Then you call for help, in Switzerland the ambulance service on **144**, and check the breathing.
